subtopic: MR. PEARSON  FAILURE TO TABLE DEPARTMENTAL REPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. PEARSON  FAILURE TO TABLE DEPARTMENTAL REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting this house. It arises from the proceedings of yesterday when we were discussing the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. We discussed those estimates without having before us the report of the department which is required by statute, under the act setting up the department. It will be found in volume II of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, as section 10 of that act. The last report from this department is for the period 1955-56; hence the provisions of the statute were not complied with when we were discussing the work of this department.
Attention was called to that fact by two members on this side of the house. Certain explanations were given, Mr. Speaker, which were not impressive, especially the explanation as to lack of facilities for printing. As perhaps some hon. members will recall, in 1945 I think it was, the report on the public accounts was not printed but was tabled, as required by statute, in manuscript form by the minister concerned. Lest anyone should think this is just a minor matter and should not be raised at this time, may I quote, in support of the seriousness of this matter, a statement made in the House of Commons on November 7, 1949, in connection with the alleged failure of a member of the government at that time to produce a report as required by statute.
I quote the remarks of the then member for Lake Centre, as recorded at page 1504 of Hansard for November 7, 1949 as follows:
Parliament has the right to expect that ministers of the crown shall live up to the provisions of statutes passed by parliament; for if these be not lived up to, parliamentary responsibility ends, and a contempt of parliament occurs which should not be permitted to pass uncensured.
Later on page 1505 the same hon. member said:
The government's action in this matter cannot be laughed off. It strikes at the vitals of our democratic system; for if we cannot rely on ministers of the crown or on the government to do those things which, under law, they are required to do, we in
the opposition, instead of being able to accept what ministers of the government say and to believe that they are carrying out their responsibilities under the law, are actually placed in a position where we must begin to wonder. I doubt whether we would have had the report yet if the commissioner had not resigned and brought the matter to a head.

speechtext: Perhaps the Prime Minister and the members of the house have read reports to the effect that in Ireland they are experiencing what is tantamount to a potato famine as the result of adverse climatic conditions, and that great distress is resulting. I ask the Prime Minister whether he has considered any way in which the government of Canada could help the Irish people, both in southern Ireland and northern Ireland, to meet the situation confronting them at the present time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbakar (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED POTATO SHORTAGE
speechtext:
Naturally there is every sympathetic feeling for the situation prevailing in Ireland. We recall that more than 100 years ago, when a similar situation was most

serious, it resulted in mass migrations from that country to the great benefit of the countries to which those migrations took place.
May I say that there has been no consideration given as yet to this matter. No representations have been made, and indeed the matter had not been brought to my attention. But I can certainly say this: that having regard to the situation, if there are within our country, as I am sure there are, available supplies which will be acceptable to all of Ireland, whether north or south-and I am using that expression advisedly-I can say, and I know the hon. gentleman will join with me, that everything that can possibly be done by our country should be done and will be done.

I should like to direct a question either to the Minister of Trade and Commerce or to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It arises out of a Canadian Press report this morning which states that with the defeat in congress of the bill to provide mineral subsidies, pressure is being increased on the President to raise tariffs on Canadian lead and zinc.
Could the minister say what representations are being made to Washington, and what progress Canada is making in preventing this undesirable step being taken?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: REPORTED PRESSURE TO INCREASE UNITED STATES TARIFFS
speechtext:
I have not seen the press report referred to, but as hon. members well know our relations with Washington are very good at this time, as instanced by the action taken by the President the other day in permitting seed grain from Canada to continue to enter the United States despite a suggestion by congress that it should be excluded.
We are confident that similar action with respect to other aspects of our trade with the United States will have the same type of considerate treatment. The people at Washington are thoroughly well informed on the Canadian point of view on all matters affecting trade between our two countries.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view

of the statement attributed to the commercial attache of the United States embassy in Ottawa in an interview with the Canadian Press, to the effect that the Canadian manufacturers are missing many opportunities to sell in the United States market and that many Canadian businessmen just do not know how to make business connections in the United States and are losing a lot of business as a result; and in view of the number of officials of his department resident in the United States, can the minister inform the house if this state of affairs exists and if so what action is being taken to correct the situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.S. COMMERCIAL ATTACHE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for sending me notice of this question. I have read the press report attributed to the commercial attach# of the United States. I do not for one minute think Canadian businessmen are missing many opportunities in the United States. Our exports from Canada to the United States increased by 2 per cent and are at a total of $2.9 billion for last year, which is a very substantial amount of trade indeed, representing 60 per cent of our exports. That would not have come about unless Canadian businessmen were particularly enterprising in selling Canadian products abroad.
With regard to the number of officials of this department in the United States, I am glad the hon. member drew attention to that matter. We have 16 representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce located at various points in the United States; in Washington, four; New York, three; Boston, one; Chicago, two; Detroit, two; Los Angeles, one; New Orleans, one; San Francisco, one; and Seattle, one, making a total of 16. These representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce are constantly in touch with Canadian businessmen pointing out to them opportunities that exist for the sale of Canadian goods in the United States. Our Canadian businessmen are showing commendable enterprise in pushing the sale of Canadian products not only in the United States but elsewhere throughout the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGRICULTURAL PROGRAM-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION THIS SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to give to the members of the committee a report on the proceedings of the special emergency meeting of the general assembly of the United Nations which was adjourned on Thursday evening last.
I have prepared a statement for the information of the members of the committee. That statement will have to do with an account of the proceedings, and then I will attempt to offer some evaluation of what was achieved there, the part the Canadian delegation attempted to play, and some ideas about the immediate and long-term future that the unanimously adopted resolution may have for the peace and security of the world.
I would begin, Mr. Chairman, by recalling very briefly why the emergency special meeting of the general assembly was convened. As we all know, Mr. Chairman, the immediate reason for holding this special emergency meeting of the general assembly was the fact that the security council on August 7 had under consideration complaints that had been made to the security council by Lebanon and by the Hashemite kingdom of Jordan concerning interference by other countries in their domestic affairs.
It had, of course, been hoped in the period immediately prior to that meeting that some means of resolving the issue involved might be found through the calling of a security council meeting of a rather special character, at which heads of state might attend and at which heads of states, great powers and others, could get together, formally and informally to discuss problems of the Middle East. Many of us had in mind that at such a meeting at a high level other countries which were not members, which were not represented on the security council but which were directly concerned with the problems of the Middle East, would be given an opportunity to present their views concerning those problems.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members will recall the Canadian government advocated the holding of such a meeting within the framework of the security council; but when it became apparent that further action in the security council was no longer possible, having regard to the lack of unanimity among the permanent members of the security council and the use of the veto by the U.S.S.R., the questions at issue were transferred to the general assembly and there was called by the U.S.S.R. an emergency special [The Deputy Chairman.]
session under the procedures envisaged in the uniting for peace resolution of November 3, 1950.
At that time the Canadian government took the stand that since a solution of the Middle East questions was still to be pursued within the United Nations framework, we were prepared to support efforts within the general assembly toward the finding of a solution of those problems.
Without going into detail of the underlying reasons for the transfer of those complaints from the security council to the general assembly, I will simply say that the Soviet union apparently decided that it might stand to gain by such a change of forum which would afford a better sounding board for propaganda steps; but I would remind the committee that the United States government had placed before the security council a proposal that a meeting of the general assembly should be held, provided that the discussions and deliberations within the security council broke down.
There were three main statements of position at the start of the general debate at the emergency session of the general assembly, and those three statements afford a background for what happened in the next 10 days. The first statement was made by the secretary general on August 8, and I would interpolate here that by that statement on August 8 at the so-called pro forma meeting of the general assembly the secretary general indeed set the tone for a constructive debate. He outlined on that occasion what he termed some of the basic needs for action in the region of the Middle East and suggested the desirability of finding a formula by which the affairs of the states of the region could be looked at very carefully and whereby they could take a more positive attitude with respect to the affairs of their neighbours.
Second, in that introductory statement he emphasized the need of finding a formula to permit a United Nations solution to the problems of Lebanon and Jordan. Third, he held forth on the need for a co-operative approach to the economic problems of the Arab Middle East. While he made no specific proposals, he succeeded on that occasion in drawing the attention of the 81 nations represented in the general assembly to the important truth that the key to the problems of the region rests largely in the hands of the states of the area themselves.
The second important contribution made to the opening discussions at the emergency session of the general assembly was made by the President of the United States of America. On August 13 he successfully attempted to translate some of the principles enunciated

by the secretary general into positive proposals. Members of the house no doubt will recall having seen references to his six points in the press. He addressed himself in a positive fashion not only to the immediate but to the long term problems of the Middle East, and I would say here that in his address to the general assembly President Eisenhower insisted at all times that any remedy for the anxious situation there and any solutions to the problems must be put forward and carried out by the United Nations. He took great care to say that he was not suggesting that the United States alone should carry out these measures, but rather would promote solutions of short term and long term problems under the aegis of the United Nations.
I would mention in this context that the President emphasized, as did the secretary general on August 8, the need to recognize the right of the peoples of the Arab nations to determine their own destinies, and he stated positively that no one could ever envisage solutions to their problems which would be permanent if they were in any manner imposed on the nations of the Middle East.
The third statement to which I should like to refer is that made by Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, who promptly endorsed President Eisenhower's remarks. That is the background which set the stage for the very constructive and profitable debate.
However, I have a fourth statement in mind to which I should like to refer. At an early stage of the meetings of the emergency session of the general assembly we had the draft resolution and supporting statements of the Soviet union. Far from attempting to broaden or build upon the constructive approach that had been made by the secretary general, the President of the United States and the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, the Soviet resolution was essentially negative, dwelling solely on the question of withdrawal of United States and United Kingdom forces from Lebanon and Jordan.
The Soviet resolution disregarded other Middle East issues, such as the economic issue and the political issue, that were directly involved in the deliberations of the security council and would have to be taken into consideration if anything constructive were to come out of the emergency session of the general assembly. Those were disregarded. The role assigned to the United Nations by the draft resolution of the U.S.S.R. would be that the secretary general would be given no opportunity to eliminate the underlying causes of tension in that area.
Supply-External Affairs
Furthermore, the accusing overtones of the statement by Mr. Gromyko when he presented the U.S.S.R. resolution, a statement which alleged aggression on the part of the United States and the United Kingdom, were clearly designed to be destructive, and held no hope or promise for reasonable and moderate discussion in the assembly free of propaganda of the cold war.
The Soviet resolution was the only one that at that time was before the emergency session of the general assembly, and may I also say here that it had no prospect of adoption because the majority of delegations recognized that this emergency session of the general assembly had been convened to do much more than simply arrange for the substitution of United Nations action for national action in Lebanon and Jordan.
That was the only resolution. By reason of that fact, the narrow and negative basis of the Soviet resolution, several countries wondered whether they could not offer to the general assembly a resolution that would be more constructive, one that would be much more satisfactory, than the one that had been proposed by the U.S.S.R.; a resolution that would lay the ground work for a comprehensive consideration of the problems of the Middle East; a resolution that would use the secretary general as its instrument, the instrument of the United Nations in this particular field of trouble and excitement; a resolution that would lay the foundations for durable peace and stability in the area.
So, as so often happens, it fell to certain middle powers to undertake the difficult task of devising a resolution which would seek to attain this objective, while at the same time taking into consideration the many widely divergent points of view and conflicting interests. So Canada and Norway found themselves playing a leading role in presenting to the general assembly a type of resolution that would be constructive and comprehensive as compared with the essentially negative one that had been presented by Mr. Gromyko of the U.S.S.R.
I seize this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to pay a tribute to the devotion and the vision of the Norwegian delegation, and I single out among that delegation the Norwegian deputy foreign minister, Mr. Hans Engen, for his hard work, his tact, and his vision with respect to the formulating of a resolution that would accomplish those objectives to which I have referred. While that was going on and we were formulating this Canadian-Norwegian resolution there were other representatives, particularly in the Afro-Asian group, who were active in drafting their own resolution which reflected their over-

Supply-External Affairs riding reoccupation with the question of troop withdrawal. The Norwegian and Canadian delegations, on the other hand, were striving, as I have indicated previously, for something much broader both in terms of assembly support and of what would enable the United Nations to attempt something by way of a permanent settlement; a resolution that would enable the United Nations, through the secretary general and otherwise, to get at the basic roots of the Middle East problem and not to deal only with the symptoms of that situation.
For our part we in the Canadian delegation kept certain principles and objectives clearly before us throughout the whole period of intense negotiation which led up to the introduction of the Canadian-Norwegian resolution, with which were associated five other sponsors. In the first place-and I dwell on this point, Mr. Chairman-we in the Canadian delegation wanted something which would command the support of the Arabs themselves; for it seemed obvious that there could be no durable settlement in the Middle East without not only the consent of the Arab countries but their active cooperation. It might have been possible- I think it would have been possible-for the Canadian-Norwegian resolution to carry the required two-thirds majority vote; but if the Arabs were opposed to that resolution, we could not look forward to any success in seeking to solve the problems of the Middle East.
The second principle that the Canadian delegation had in mind always-and I say again throughout the intensive negotiations- was that regional support alone, the support of the Arab countries, would not be enough or would not suffice without the complementary support and co-operation of the great powers, all of whom are committed in various ways in the disputes of the Middle East.
Third, the Canadian delegation was intent upon finding a reasonable solution satisfactory to all the principal states concerned to cover the problem that had been brought forward on many occasions, the problem of troop withdrawal. This would have to be something which would give to the United Nations and particularly to the secretary general a central role without, however, confining the mandate to the narrow issue of troop withdrawal.
It would at the same time-I refer to the draft resolution-we hoped create a situation by which the United Nations would be enabled to exert a benevolent and constructive influence not only in the present but in the future in the Middle East, through helping to establish an economic institution for the collective benefit of the Arab states and to provide perhaps an economic undergirding

-economics and politics are closely interlocked and intertwined-that would make for a new and happier basis for the relations not only among themselves but with the neighbouring states in the area. I say "among themselves". I am, of course, referring to the Arab nations; and I reiterate, not only to provide a new and happier basis for relations among themselves but also with the neighbouring states in the area.
We did not expect necessarily to have all these principles and objectives set forth in detail in the resolution. But what the Canadian delegation wanted was to find a starting point from which the objectives which I have endeavoured to describe here today could be pursued.
We were aware at the outset that we would have to rely on the ability and good offices of the secretary general to carry out both the letter and the spirit of the draft resolution. I will not attempt to recount in detail the long and intensive negotiations which went into the formulation of the seven power draft presented on August 18. We will look at the draft for a moment, but in a general way.
May I say that the draft was revised at least seven times as to context, which will indicate the care given to the particular views advanced by the various countries and groups of countries from time to time. At one time we believed we had a workable resolution, but then the attitude of the distinguished delegate from Jordan certainly surprised us and seemed to make it impossible for us to carry out the design which we had prepared for our resolution. Members of the committee may recall that the representative of Jordan in his statement to the general assembly appeared to reject any substantial role for the United Nations within Jordan, and he seemed to oppose on behalf of his government the presence of any United Nations representatives or any United Nations instrumentality within the territorial boundaries of his country with one possible exception, and one had to look through a magnifying glass to discern that exception. However, that roadblock was removed within 24 hours, when the Jordanian representative subsequently modified his position.
The essential elements of the resolution which we co-sponsored may be described in these words. It reaffirmed that all member states of the United Nations should refrain from action which might impair the freedom, independence or integrity of any state, which might cause civil strife or subvert the will of the people in any state; and it called upon all member states to observe these obligations especially in the area in question. It requested

the secretary general to make such practical arrangements after consultation with the governments concerned as were deemed necessary, and who could do this better than the secretary general? But he would have to do it on the spot.
May I refer for the moment to the U.S.S.R. resolution in this context. That resolution instructed the secretary general to go to Lebanon and Jordan for the purpose of supervising the withdrawal of troops, and nothing more. But our resolution, and I am not giving away any secrets when I say this, met with the entire satisfaction of the secretary general, although it imposed a great load upon him. In our final resolution the secretary general was to make such practical arrangements as he, in consultation with the governments concerned, might find would adequately serve to help in upholding the purposes and principles of the charter in relation to Lebanon and Jordan in the circumstances obtaining at the time in those countries.
In our resolution the question of withdrawal of the troops of the United States and the United Kingdom was not the subject of a specific provision, but in the preambular clause it was noted by the general assembly that declarations were addressed to the president of the general assembly in the letters written to him on August 18 by the representatives of the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom, in which they stated their willingness and desire to withdraw from Lebanon and Jordan respectively when the United Nations could take effective action to ensure, without regard to any regime or political party, stability and security in those countries.
Therefore the resolution sponsored by Norway, Canada and the five other countries did not, as I have said, expressly refer to withdrawals but implicitly made provision for the withdrawal of those forces by ensuring the mandate of the secretary general in the light of the United States and United Kingdom declarations as contained in the letters to which I have referred.
Finally, the seven power draft resolution -the Canada-Norway resolution-invited the secretary general to continue his studies with respect to the feasibility of establishing a stand-by United Nations peace force. Hon. members will recall that in this house during the earlier discussion on external affairs I expressed the view of the government in that regard, and we welcomed the insertion of a reference to a stand-by force.
In the seven power resolution there was also a statement to the effect that careful study would be given to the question of
Supply-External Affairs economic development in the countries of the Middle East, and it urged the Arab countries in explicit terms to study the representations made to them by the secretary general, which were endorsed by the President of the United States. It also requested the member states to co-operate fully in the carrying out of those studies and to assist in implementing the more positive and operative parts of the resolution. Finally, it invited the secretary general to report on his activities in trying to establish agreement among the Arab countries, the first of such reports being required to be made to the general assembly by not later than September 30, 1958.
While the seven power draft does conform to the principles and does meet the main objectives which had governed the Canadian approach, we were at the same time conscious of the shortcomings of that resolution. I endeavoured to make it clear, on behalf not only of Canada but of the other co-sponsors, in my statement in support of the resolution on August 19, 1958 that we were open to constructive suggestions with respect to its improvement. I stated particularly and at once that if it were to serve to secure great power and regional support we immediately conceded that the resolution could not be considered by any country or group of countries as perfect. In the atmosphere which prevailed on Tuesday of this week however, this resolution undoubtedly offered the only common denominator which would warrant broad support as a formula for the reconciliation of conflicting interests.
I referred once again at that stage to the negative aspect of the other resolution which had been tabled by the U.S.S.R. I stated on behalf of Canada that our resolution could serve as a point of departure to reconcile some of the conflicting interests, and expressed the hope that it would serve as a basis for discussion. It must be remembered that we had been negotiating for nearly a week and nothing positive had been put before the assembly in terms of a resolution. There was nothing of that kind on which to centre the attention of the general assembly other than the unsatisfactory and negative Soviet resolution.
There was a general and intense will- we could sense it-in the meetings of the general assemby to study anything which seemed to carry with it a plan for the future and not just a consideration of past events. This resolution gave a new focal point on Tuesday afternoon for the attention of the representatives of the nations who were in that hall on that occasion. In my statement

Supply-External Affairs in support of the resolution I frankly admitted-and I say this for the third time in words other than those I have already used-the shortcomings of the text which was presented in the resolution, but I say without any conceit and without any lack of modesty that I have reason to believe that these observations by Canada's delegation gave some hope for a common point of view coming out of the Arab ranks.
While the debate on the Canadian-Norwegian resolution was taking place on Wednesday there occurred what was indeed a dramatic and sudden reappraisal from the Arab ranks as a whole, though I would say it was not entirely a surprise to some of us. This led to the submission of a new draft resolution to the assembly by all ten Arab states, and this new development altered the whole basis on which the assembly's discussion had been proceeding and led rapidly, on Thursday evening, to a unanimous vote in favour of the Arab resolution.
Canada, and indeed all the sponsors, and the United States, the United Kingdom, France and other great powers immediately expressed their willingness and happiness to join with us, the co-sponsors of the Cana-dian-Norwegian resolution, in this new development. Therefore it was particularly fitting, in the light of the article in the charter regarding the regional settlement of disputes, that it should have been the Arabs themselves who came up with this formula and provided a starting point for working out a solution to the issues which have wracked the Arab world and on more than one occasion have threatened the peace of the whole world. I am satisfied that the resolution meets most of the main objectives which the co-sponsors of the seven power resolution had in mind and, in fact, it draws heavily on the letter and the spirit of the seven power resolution which we had cosponsored.
The Arab resolution contains three main elements. First, it reaffirms pledges already given by the Arab states that they will respect the systems of government established in the Arab states, and it calls on all members of the United Nations to conform with the principles of mutual respect for each other's integrity and non-interference in each other's affairs. This passage corresponds very closely in meaning to a similar passage of the seven-power resolution, but it expresses itself in terms which are more precise and which have a more particular relevance to the Arab and Asian world.
Second, the Arab resolution requests the secretary general to make such practical arrangements as would adequately help in upholding the purposes of the charter in

relation to Lebanon and Jordan in the present circumstances. These are the exact words of the seven power resolution. But the Arab resolution, unlike the Norwegian-Canadian formula on withdrawal, refers expressly and exclusively to withdrawal in the text of the resolution in the words "and thereby facilitate the early withdrawal of foreign troops from the two countries". This is a more direct formula for dealing with the crucial question of troop withdrawals than had been attempted in the seven power draft, and I would remind those who might wish to scrutinize too carefully the wording of this section-"and thereby facilitate the early withdrawal of foreign troops from the two countries"-that this formula was accepted willingly by the United States and by the United Kingdom.
May I quote to the committee the words of the secretary of state of the United States when he said they would heartily endorse the Arab resolution. These are his words:
The United States rejoices at the prospective assumption by the United Nations of the responsibility which we reluctantly assumed in an emergency and are eager to lay down.
He was followed immediately by the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom who stated, in effect, that the quicker the practical arrangements contemplated in the resolution could be made on a realistic basis, and here I quote, "the sooner it will be possible for us to withdraw our troops". The Lebanese and the Jordanians accepted this Arab resolution voluntarily, and the United Arab Republic pledged its earnest support for the fulfilment of the engagements which were set out in the resolution relating to this matter. I shall return to this point in a moment.
The third element in the resolution consists of a repetition of the provision in the seven power resolution inviting the secretary-general to continue his study with a view to possible assistance regarding an Arab development institution in the economic field, and to provide for this under amicable political arrangements.
I say frankly that there are two elements which I would like to have seen included in the Arab resolution. In my statement in the general assembly in support of the Cana-dian-Norwegian resolution I expressed the hope that there might be concluded an interlocking network of non-aggression agreements which would guarantee the independence and integrity of each and all of the Middle East states. I had in mind particularly the relations of the Arab states with their non-Arab neighbours.

That is not in the resolution. Members of this committee will be glad to hear, however, that from the remarks of some of the Arab leaders representing several of the Arab countries, made in support of their resolution, there is reason to hope that the cordial relations now established among the Arab states will be carried forward into their individual and collective relations with non-Arab states of the region. I look upon this as a result which can logically flow-and in some measure I expect it-from the activities which the United Nations through its secretary general will shortly be undertaking in this area.
The only feature of the seven-power resolution which failed to reappear in the Arab resolution was the reference to the United Nations peace force. That is not in the Arab resolution, whereas it was in our resolution. The text of that part of our resolution urged the secretary general to continue his studies with respect to the establishment of a peace force under the flag of the United Nations, and our purpose was to insist that this item be on the agenda of the thirteenth regular session of the general assembly which will begin on September 16.
I must admit, however, that in a resolution dealing with the Middle East situation it is hardly relevant to put in a paragraph that refers to a United Nations agency that could operate not only in the Middle East but throughout the world. I assure hon. gentlemen of this committee, however, that this omission need not be regarded as significant. It has been definitely stated that it will be on the agenda of the thirteenth regular session of the general assembly to which I have referred. To have pressed it at that time which I should like to have done on behalf of the Canadian delegation, would have revived widespread anxieties concerning the use of force for the settlement of international disputes, even though that force would operate under the United Nations flag. Bringing in that extraneous matter might have delayed a solution which holds out the promise of a settlement of disputes in relation to a particular area. But I say this very carefully, Mr. Chairman; it is a matter which deserves extremely careful study.
I should warn hon. members of the committee that I was conscious of a deep division of opinion within the assembly on this whole question of a stand-by force, a division that grew deeper and deeper during the succeeding days of the debate. There are many practical problems to be faced, not the least of which will be a decision as to who should be the final arbiter of when political or military circumstances would justify the use of a United Nations armed force. This was
Supply-External Affairs impressed upon me as the debate proceeded. But I say again it is now under study by officials of the United Nations, and there will be an opportunity to consider this more carefully in the meetings of the assembly that will begin next month. It is the armed aspect, the police aspect, of any proposal that would carry with it the suggestion that it should operate under the flag of the United Nations that worries many of the nations, small and great.
I look upon the Arab resolution as an evolution from and fulfilment of the seven power resolution with which Canada had been associated and one, moreover, which holds out better prospects for peace in the Middle East. Why? Because this formula and this resolution have come out of and were proposed by the Arab states themselves, and have won the unanimous support of all members of the United Nations including- and I would emphasize the importance of this-the approval of all the great powers. Mr. Gromyko expressed his intention to vote for the Arab resolution. He could not afford to do otherwise. He could not afford to vote against the Arab resolution; yet at the same time he fell back on propaganda and said, "This is really what we were after when we called for the emergency session of the general assembly". And so we have regional support, indeed a regional genesis, of the Arab resolution and we have the approval of the great powers. It was a unanimous decision. That is one of the principles we in the Canadian delegation had in mind when we began, in association with the Norwegians, to formulate a positive, creative and comprehensive resolution to present to the assembly.
The secretary general will be leaving for the Middle East on Monday afternoon. I saw him yesterday at a luncheon, and I could say that despite the inherent modesty of the man he has a certain self-confidence with respect to the success of the role that he will play in the next one or two weeks in the Middle East that will be of assistance to him in translating into practical and successful action the mandate he has received from the assembly. In accepting that mandate the secretary general is adding to the already heavy burden of responsibility which he has been called upon to assume in recent weeks, and none of us should underestimate the difficulties or delicacy of the new tasks we are asking him to assume. This is related to the solution of these problems.
The fact that his mandate is a broad one, leaving him wide discretion to consult and act on his own initiative as circumstances may require, is a tribute indeed to the confidence which the assembly, speaking

Supply-External Affairs with a unanimous voice, reposes in his skill and integrity. I am sure I reflect the opinion of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this house when I say Canada shares in that confidence in the secretary general. We must now hope most earnestly that the unanimity that was found in New York will be fully reflected in a co-operative attitude on the part of all states concerned in order that the United Nations, which the secretary general so wonderfully symbolizes, will be successful in bringing about a new era of peace and stability in the Middle East.
The unanimous adoption of the Arab resolution has been eminently satisfactory, but we now need deeds. I am not discounting my hope and indeed my expectation when I say that now is the time for deeds on the part of the states concerned to achieve a practical realization of that resolution. As the secretary general leaves New York on Monday afternoon I hope he will carry with him the thoughts and prayers of everyone who voted for that resolution.
I have referred to certain documents, resolutions and a declaration of intention, and for the benefit of hon. members of the committee I now propose to table them.
I have one further reference to the present international situation. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that there were two events yesterday in many ways of equal significance to the unanimous adoption by the emergency session of the general assembly of the Arab resolution. Those two events were the announcements on the part of the United States and the United Kingdom to the effect that they would be willing on October 31 to begin negotiations with the U.S.S.R. for an agreement that would provide for the cessation of nuclear tests. That would be a tripartite agreement or two bilateral agreements. I have expressed the hope that those agreements could be sealed under the United Nations.
I would remind the members of the committee, Mr. Chairman, that for several months the Canadian government has urged that such an agreement should be entered into, and that is why we urged the holding of a meeting of nuclear scientists at Geneva. We had hoped that in a cool atmosphere the scientists could find a satisfactory arrangement with respect to the detection of nuclear tests which would lead and indeed point the way to a political agreement in that regard. No doubt Canada, geographically speaking, must be used to station the equipment or instruments or whatever techniques have been suggested by the scientists at Geneva, but as the Prime Minister said yesterday Canada will be eager and willing to do her part in implementing such an agreement. That

is not disarmament, Mr. Chairman, but it points the way to disarmament. It prevents further armament, if you allow me to put it that way.
We had hoped, Mr. Chairman, that within the next few months it will be possible to convene a group of experts, such as those who met at Geneva in the last few months, who would study control techniques and control devices that would prevent the possibility of surprise attack. With that hope and the statements yesterday of the United States and the United Kingdom with respect to their proposals to the U.S.S.R. and the unanimous decision of the emergency general session of the general assembly, I feel better about the international situation than I have felt since I became a member of this house. But words will not be enough.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first words must be those of appreciation to the minister for the statement he has just given us, and words of welcome home to him from the United Nations special assembly which has just completed its work. I know how hard he must have been working there in recent days. I know what it involves in terms of preparation of public statements, and I know what it involves in terms of working behind the scenes. I suspect that last week-end he did a good deal of that, not only working behind the scenes but constructing scenes behind which to work, plugging loopholes in the scenes as he got them constructed, and trying to get people to work with him behind those scenes.
The result of all that activity was the introduction of a resolution in the assembly later in the week by the delegation of Norway, headed by a very distinguished man with whom I have had the privilege of working in the past. It must have been, I think, in a way disappointing to my hon. friend and to the other sponsor of that resolution that at the last moment, it was replaced by the Arab resolution which, to my way of thinking, was not as effective for the purpose for which it was designed as the seven power resolution but which for other reasons was perhaps inevitable. I shall have something to say about that later.
I know also that the minister in his work in the United Nations, indeed in his work in the department, has had the advantage of the services of a highly skilled body of experts. This, Mr. Chairman, gives me the opportunity to pay my tribute to the work of the Department of External Affairs both at home and abroad, and to the work of the officials in that department at all levels of official activity. I know from the records of the committee on external affairs-indeed, from

the meetings I attended-that the work of the department is continuing to expand. Important new offices are being opened and I am sure that is all necessary; and if it is necessary it is desirable. I do remember, however, that not so many years ago the expansion of the activities of the Department of External Affairs in the opening of embassies abroad was greeted in some quarters in this house with some hesitation as unnecessary extravagance.
I am quite certain that no governmental work is more important to the people of Canada than that of the Department of External Affairs, dealing as it does with our relations with other countries in this difficult and critical time in the world's history. I know we are very fortunate in this country -and I am sure the minister will agree with me-in having a foreign service second to none in the world to help him in that work.
We have built up over the years in that department a great body of professional help. One reason, I may suggest, why the department does operate effectively as I think it does, is that it has been made clear from the beginning that the headship of every post in the foreign service of Canada from the most junior, from the least important mission abroad to the most important mission, is open to any member of that service who may qualify for that position; and that there has been no interference of any kind in the work and in the legitimate ambitions of the members of the service. I hope, and I know, it will continue that way.
The minister quite rightly has confined his remarks largely to the work of the special assembly and I shall have something to say about that. I should also like, however, to take advantage of this opportunity-it may be the last opportunity that we shall have-to discuss some other aspects of external affairs and deal with one or two other matters. But first, Mr. Chairman, let me deal with the work of the special assembly which the minister has covered.
I continue to believe, and I suspect that the minister would not be in too violent disagreement with me, that the best method of dealing with what has been called the Middle East crisis, which arose out of events in Iraq, Lebanon and later in Jordan, would have been a small, informal, confidential conference at the summit, to use the expression we have come to use now; a conference which in its representation would consist of those most concerned, a conference which might possibly have elaborated policies which would have prevented this kind of thing and which would prevent a recurrence of it in the future. When I have advocated that machinery for dealing with this crisis I have
Supply-External Affairs not had in mind, of course, that this involved in any way the by-passing of the states most directly concerned, the Arab states and Israel, or the by-passing of smaller states generally. Nevertheless it will not be possible at the United Nations or elsewhere to work out policies which will result in stability, progress and peace in this part of the world unless the major powers can get together and try to co-ordinate their policies in that region.
I thought and I continue to think that the head of the Soviet government, Mr. Khrushchev, gave us a remarkably good opportunity to make or at least attempt to make some progress in that direction when he invited the heads of the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States, France and India and the secretary general of the United Nations to join him in that kind of conference. I still think this invitation should have been seized upon as preliminary to the kind of discussion that would later take place in the general assembly of the United Nations. As we all know, that invitation bogged down through a complicated exchange of diplomatic notes, a maze of correspondence, and eventually Mr. Khrushchev escaped from what I believe was an increasingly embarrassing situation for him, after he had second thoughts as to the kind of meeting he had invited, consisting of representatives of the three western powers, a friendly member of the commonwealth and the secretary general, by switching the invitation, because of the delay on all sides in doing anything about his first proposal, to a meeting of the general assembly which as the minister pointed out, had already been put forward from other quarters.
The minister said in his observations that perhaps Mr. Khrushchev thought he might have something to gain from transferring the discussions to the general assembly. I am inclined to think that Mr. Khrushchev might not have had, on the other hand, a completely free hand in his action at that time because it took place, as the committee knows, shortly after the visit he paid to Mao Tse-tung in Peking. It might well have been that at that meeting the Chinese communist leader, recognizing that Mohammed could not go to the mountain and the mountain could not go to Mohammed, decided that there would not be a mountain at all so instead of a summit conference, an emergency meeting of the 81-nation general assembly was held, on which the minister has reported. The London Economist, a magazine from which some of us often quote and which a good many of us read, had this to say in the first paragraph of its leading article on August 9:
The summit seems to have vanished like a Middle East mirage. Instead of scaling exhilarating peaks

Supply-External Affairs the summiteers face the prospect of plodding through the vast and dusty expanse of the 81-member United Nations assembly. To come down to earth so abruptly and land in this field full of folk is enough to make anybody feel flat; and it is hardly surprising that all concerned are scouring the plain for scapegoats.
As the minister has pointed out, the results of this meeting on the plain were better than that. Indeed some of the things that many people, myself among them I confess, feared from a meeting of this kind, that it would degenerate into an exchange of propaganda insults and be completely negative in character, did not, thank goodness, materialize. Perhaps we owe a debt of gratitude for that result especially to the President of the United States, who in his opening statement set the tone of the meeting on a pretty high level. Therefore the results, although they may not have been all that we hoped for or, indeed, that the minister and the government hoped for, were certainly not those which might have been feared.
It is perfectly true that as a result of the emergency session of the United Nations assembly the sense of crisis which we had a few weeks ago has diminished. In my view, however, it is also true that the underlying problems which served to produce the crisis have not been dealt with. What the United Nations assembly has done is give the governments concerned another chance to deal with these problems.
The minister, speaking from the United Nations in New York, was quoted in the press last night-I think he used the same expression this morning-as saying that the Arab resolution is regarded as eminently satisfactory, and according to this report he went on to say, although I do not think he went so far this morning:
All delegations will feel a sense of gratification at the respect for the charter that has been demonstrated-
I think we can all subscribe to that.
-and at the happier era now lying before the Arab states in their mutual relations.
I hope he is right. If the wording of the Arab resolution is carried into action, and the minister was careful to make this condition, then perhaps we can look forward to that result. I am quoting this statement because I have the text of it and perhaps will be more accurate in my references to it than I would be if I were to try to remember the exact words the minister used this morning. The minister went on to say:
All of these-
Certain considerations he had mentioned.
-are adequately met by the Arab resolution. It provides a satisfactory code to govern the mutual relations of the Arab states.

From my reading of the resolution I think that is correct, but I would point out to the minister, undoubtedly he does not need to have it pointed out to him, that this satisfactory code which is embodied in the resolution, at least in paragraph (a) of the resolution, the code to which he was referring, is taken from a previous pact setting up the league of Arab states and in its second paragraph, if I am not wrong, from the Bandung resolution. Therefore this particular code which is now embodied in the resolution in this form has already been in existence for some years. So we can only hope that putting it in a United Nations resolution which has been accepted by every member of the United Nations will in fact provide a better opportunity for using it to govern relations between these states than has been the case in recent years. To that extent I think we can all take a good deal of satisfaction from the resolution.
But, Mr. Chairman, the fact remains, as I said a moment ago, that the underlying problems which brought about this trouble in the first place are still there. The United Nations activitiy in this regard has been beneficial. There is no doubt about that. But I am not sure that the United Nations assembly on this occasion is not in about the same situation as it was a couple of years ago over Suez, when we were I think able down there to resolve an immediate crisis but did not take advantage of the atmosphere of crisis to get down to the problems that brought about the crisis.
And so we find ourselves in the same situation on this occasion. This Arab resolution was essential perhaps to resolve the immediate crisis, and perhaps it has done that. However, it will not be successful unless these basic problems are dealt with. As the minister and other members of the government must know, in these international matters once the immediate crisis passes we are inclined to forget the situation which brought it about, and to do nothing about it until we have another crisis. I hope that will not happen on this occasion.

Yes; in a sense I think they are a continuation of those which were in existence two years ago. Some of them perhaps are new, but certainly some of them were in existence then. I will mention one or two of them. The first one that occurs to

my mind is the inability-and I make no criticism of anybody or any country in this regard-the demonstrated inability in this crisis to take any action that would improve relations between Israel and her Arab neighbours. It does not seem that we are going to escape from this dangerous situation in the Middle East unless something is done about that matter. When I say that, I have no illusions about the difficulty in that regard.

Yes, I did appreciate it. As I said, in making these particular references and giving these illustrations I am not attempting to be critical in any way of what the government did or did not do at the United Nations assembly. I am quite aware of the fact that this matter could not have been dealt with at this special assembly at the United Nations, and I am quite aware of the fact that the minister referred to it. I read his speech in regard to that matter. He made reference to it in a way which I thought was helpful.
Nevertheless, until the international assembly and the governments most concerned are able to do something in a constructive and practical way about this matter, I am afraid we shall continue to move from critical situation to critical situation. While this is not easy of accomplishment, I hope that perhaps we shall soon be able to make progress in this particular issue of the relations between Israel and its neighbours because, as I say, it is rather basic to the whole situation out there.
Then there is the economic situation as mentioned in this Arab resolution. It was mentioned more effectively, I think, in the seven power resolution. I do not see how the nations of the Middle East area can really work together on these economic matters which are so important unless some recognition is given to the position of Israel in this regard. So here is another example of the interrelationship of politics and economics.
Then there is the question-the minister mentioned it this morning, and he certainly tried to do something about it in New York- of United Nations machinery. I am not now thinking of economic machinery, but of United Nations political machinery. He does not like the word "police" and I know why. It arouses the wrong kind of feeling in certain quarters. My reference is to the recognition
Supply-External Affairs of the importance of some United Nations political machinery which will be available to be moved into areas of difficulty. The minister pointed out that this is a complicated and difficult business, and that there are nations represented at New York who are worried about the principle involved, namely that of putting force behind the United Nations. No doubt some smaller countries are afraid that, if that is done, the force could be used against their interests.
But while there are difficulties, and I appreciate them, surely they are not of a kind to prevent us from trying to bring about a situation in which we shall have some permanent stand-by United Nations police machinery. I am not thinking of a United Nations force of the type we discussed in 1945, 1946 and 1947, in which would be included contingents from the great powers. That is an impossibility in the present situation. I am not even thinking about Trygve Lie's United Nations police force, his legion or whatever he called it. I am thinking now-and I have mentioned this many times previously, as have other members-of the desirability of setting up a central headquarters in New York of the kind which we were obliged to set up so quickly for the Suez operation, and the desirability of governments making available on request to that headquarters of the United Nations a force which might be required for a particular operation.
The minister said that one of the difficulties was as to who would make the decision, and how it would be made, which would bring this kind of machinery into action. Of course that is a difficulty. But I have in mind only having those forces available when that decision has been made. We have now had two or three illustrations of how it can be done, and also some of the jurisdictional problems of a force of this kind, and of the agency governing the force, have been worked out in practice. It is now fairly clear that you cannot use a force of this kind for any purpose whatever except by agreement at the United Nations and by agreement with the country in which the force operates. Although it has difficulties and although it has handicaps, it is an important thing to do. The minister himself has underlined the importance of this.
I was glad to hear him say that while in this Arab resolution there is no reference to a force of that kind, although there was a reference in the seven power resolution, nevertheless this matter is to come up for consideration at the next assembly. That will be meeting in two or three weeks. I would hope that this matter will be considered as one of the priority items on the

Supply-External Affairs agenda, and that we shall be able to make some effective progress in that regard. The fact that it is not mentioned in the Arab resolution is a little disappointing, in my opinion, but perhaps not too important in view of the fact that it will be discussed.
The Arab resolution, which I have before me and which I think is not as good a resolution as the seven power one but which I recognize had a certain advantage in the fact that it obtained unanimous support, which I doubt the seven power resolution would have obtained, does, as the minister pointed out, lay down this pledge of non-interference. This pledge has already been given previously but it is good to have it repeated in a resolution which was passed unanimously by the United Nations assembly.
It is a strange clause, if I may say so, to an outsider who has not been concei'ned with drafting it. I know what goes on down there in the drafting of resolutions, and the changes that have to be made until the final resolution sometimes is understandable only to those who have been in from the beginning. The first operative paragraph of this resolution, or the part of it which I shall read, is as follows: The United Nations assembly-
-welcomes the renewed assurances given by the Arab states to observe the provisions of article 8 of the pact of the league of Arab states that "each member state shall respect the systems of government established in the other member states and regard them as exclusive concerns of those states" and that-
And here is another quotation.
-each shall pledge to abstain from any action calculated to change established systems of government.
The normal and obvious interpretation of this is that they pledge themselves not to change even their own form of government, but I take it that is not what is meant by the resolution. Then in paragraph 2 there is a very interesting phrase which could be used to facilitate the development of the economies of the Arab states and to facilitate what surely is essential if there is to be stability in that area in some form namely the equalization of resources and income and wealth among the various states. There is a reference in this agreement which might be used for that purpose, and that is the one calling upon all Arab states to act strictly in accordance with the principle-I am leaving out some of the words-"of equal and mutual benefit." If that were to be put into effect among the Arab states some very important changes indeed would be required.
In the Arab resolution, as the minister pointed out-and this is in contrast to the seven power resolution-there is in a rather complicated and ambiguous fashion a reference to early withdrawal of foreign troops [Mr. Pearson.?

from the two countries, Lebanon and Jordan. No one should take exception to that, because that is the declared policy of the two countries whose forces are presently stationed in these countries.
I think we can hope that this withdrawal will be brought about as quickly as possible. I wish to return, however, to the desirability of pressing ahead in the United Nations to set up the machinery so that if we face this kind of problem in the future, or something similar to it, that there will be something upon which the United Nations can count for quick action.
The President of the United States had something to say on this matter at a press conference two days ago. I was a little discouraged, perhaps unnecessarily so, by his remarks when he was questioned about it. He is reported in the New York Times of August 21, 1958 as saying the following with reference to a United Nations stand-by force:
-it is one of those things that I think has to develop and to come about with the growth of common sense and a little bit greater spirit of tolerance among nations.
I think it is a very fine thing. I think it is one of those things that probably will not be done exactly at this moment.
I agree that it will not be done exactly at this moment, but I do hope it will not be delayed too long, because I think it would serve a very useful purpose, if only as a foundation for the effort to put force behind our law and establish a more effective way of dealing with these matters in the future.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Having regard to his experience in 1945, 1946 and 1947, to which he made reference, I am sure he will agree that at that time we felt there should be set up some international force. Would he consider it amiss if I ask him what actually happened to deny the achievement of those hopes which were so apparent at San Francisco? What was the reason no action was taken?

speechtext:
I attended the meeting of the committee at San Francisco dealing with this aspect of the charter. When the charter was drafted at San Francisco it was felt that the countries having the greatest responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security were the permanent members of the security council. Any force behind the charter would therefore have to come primarily, though not exclusively, from those permanent members of the security council. If they could agree on the development of an international peace force of this type, with British, United States, Russian and Chinese forces, there would indeed be something which could keep the peace.

Such a force, however, could not go into operation without a decision of the security council, not the assembly. As each security council member had a veto, no decision could be taken unless they were all in agreement. It became clear that they would not be in agreement shortly after the charter was drafted and therefore the machinery which was set up, as I said in the last debate in this house on external affairs, is still formally in existence; the military committee of representatives of the permanent members of the council, this machinery was never able to operate, not even to the point where a plan could be produced for an international police force. There was a Russian member on that committee.
As the futility of the security council as an agency for putting force behind the law became more and more apparent, we had to fall back upon the assembly, where the veto does not operate. As hon. members know, recognition of the necessity for that change was given when we passed the uniting for peace resolution in the assembly, in 1950, and any action that has been taken since that time in this field has been under that resolution through the general assembly, where only a two thirds majority is required. Action is therefore limited, because without the cooperation of the great powers it is idle to talk about any large force to maintain peace.
No United Nations police force of the kind I have mentioned could do that, of course. But what it could do, this is something which has been recommended many times in this house by many hon. members, including the Prime Minister himself, is move into disputed areas under the flag of the United Nations, to represent the international communities in those areas of disturbance, those areas which are uneasy under an armistice settlement agreed upon by governments, in order to make sure that those settlements are observed and that the disturbances do not erupt into violence.
This has been done in the Suez area during the last year and a half. The United Nations observers are not doing the same kind of work, though not working under the same circumstances as outlined above but those observers have been effective in another way in Lebanon. The same kind of thing is being done, though again in a different way, on the borders between Pakistan, and India and though not immediately under the United Nations but still representing the international community, a very effective job has been done in Indo-China.
This, however, is not the kind of thing we had in mind at San Francisco when, hoping that the great powers would work
Supply-External Affairs together to prevent any outbreak such as that through which we had just passed during world war II, we thought at least we would have enough force behind a United Nations organization not only to prevent small skirmishes growing, if there were small skirmishes, but also to enforce law by an overwhelming force which would be at the disposal of the international organization. As has been said by a justice of the United States supreme court, this is still a gleaming dream of peace, but it is not even within the bounds of realization at the present time. So we have to fall back on the kind of thing the minister is talking about and which is going to be discussed at the next assembly, which I hope will result in some progress.
There was one other aspect of the assembly deliberations which caused some uneasiness to me which was perhaps also felt by other hon. members of this house. That was the tendency in certain quarters to assume that it is the function, the duty and the obligation of the United Nations to do something about indirect aggression, and that if we could not deal with indirect aggression we would not be able to deal with direct aggression. Indeed, we are not so likely to have direct aggression but are much more likely to have trouble arising out of indirect aggression,-the interference of one country in the affairs of another country in order to bring about a change in the status of that country.
I know that we all realize that this is the way the communists operate, and it is quite likely that we may not be faced in the near future with the dropping of hydrogen bombs but with infiltrations across borders, economic, political and social. It is important to try to do something about this, but I think we are on pretty dubious ground when we try to have discussions of the kind we had in the United Nations special assembly in this crisis in the Middle East on the necessity of dealing with indirect aggression through some form of the United Nations machinery. We might as well be frank about it; every great power does use its influence across the borders of other countries to bring about in those countries a state of affairs which will make those other countries more friendly to the power whose aim it is to aggress in this indirect way.
Russia and other communist states make this a major instrument of their national policy; there is no doubt about that. But when we accuse them-and we have every right to accuse them-and when we ask the United Nations to do something about that kind of aggression, we invite the kind of retaliation which we undoubtedly will get in the United Nations assembly. Nobody is

Supply-External Affairs guiltless, and I do not think it will get us anywhere in terms of United Nations resolutions.
Yesterday I read in the press that the United States congress had appropriated another $10 million for the "Voice of America" to increase the effectiveness of its broadcasts to other countries, perhaps to the Arab world and behind the iron curtain. No doubt this is desirable if we can get to the people of those countries, but the governments of those countries perhaps consider it, quite unjustly from our point of view, a form of indirect aggression. Therefore any effort to make too much out of this at the United Nations merely involves charges and countercharges and does not get us very far.
There are two or three other matters I want to discuss, and perhaps the minister will be able to deal with some of the points I venture to raise. The first is the situation with regard to NATO. The United Nations has at the present time once again shown its indisputable value under the leadership of its secretary general. I was going to say "under the leadership of its indispensable secretary general". We have learned over the last two or three years that there are no indispensable men, but if there is any man who is near to being indispensable, however, it is, I suggest, the secretary general of the United Nations; and the value of his leadership has been well demonstrated. However, we must not forget that another of our defences-and I am talking now of military, not political, defence-is the North Atlantic treaty organization. Anything which weakens that organization weakens our defences until we can do away with that organization entirely and bring defence under the United Nations, and we are a long way from that.
All members of this committee are, I am sure, worried about disputes within the North Atlantic treaty organization. The minister said on another occasion, and I was glad to hear him say it, that political consultation within the NATO council was closer and more constructive today than perhaps it had ever been before. That is all to the good, and there is a blueprint in the report of a NATO committee which does, I think, lay down the lines on which such consultation can be effected. We have to develop this kind of consultation, both political and economic, or NATO will not ultimately survive.
But against these more hopeful signs of the development of consultation must be set the fact that within the NATO circle there are dangerous disputes between NATO members.
I note one major dispute, over Cyprus, in which three members of NATO are involved, perhaps more than three. The Prime Minister


of the United Kingdom has recently been making imaginative efforts to bring this conflict to an end. It is a little depressing to realize that there are so many British troops required in Cyprus and that this might be one of the reasons, though not the only one, of course, why Britain has had to cut down her forces on the continent of Europe.
That is one dispute. Another concerns Algeria. Algeria is geographically inside the NATO area and an attack on Algeria, we might remind ourselves, is an attack on Canada within the terms of the North Atlantic pact. Therefore it is a matter of immediate concern that we should do all we can to help find a solution to this problem. I think all members of this committee must have been struck by the imaginative, constructive, and liberal-spelled with a small "1"-approach to this question by General De Gaulle. Let us hope he will be successful in solving this dispute. It is not a NATO dispute in the sense that two NATO countries are involved, but it is to the extent that one country which is an important member of NATO has had to bring most of its troops from the NATO line and send them across the Mediterranean. It is a dispute which involves NATO in that sense.
Then unfortunately there has developed in the last few weeks a dispute between two NATO countries, Iceland and the United Kingdom, which cannot do anything but cause distress among other NATO members and, indeed, in other countries as well. The origin of this affair arises out of a decision of the Icelandic government made under an Icelandic act to assert control of the continental shelf, something which was agreed to at the recent Geneva conference in so far as the exploitation of the resources under the sea is concerned.
Operating under this act the government of Iceland has extended its territorial waters to 12 miles from shore and in doing so has come into conflict-according to the reports, bitter conflict-with the United Kingdom, which historically has claimed fishing and other rights on the high seas up to the three mile limit. The press tells us that a United Kingdom trawler fleet is going off in a few days to its fishing grounds which are now, under Icelandic law, within the territorial waters of Iceland, and we also read in the press that if there should be any interference with the British trawlers the necessary naval protection will be given to the British vessels. That is unhappy reading for any member of the North Atlantic treaty organization which values its relationships with both Britain and Iceland.

As is inevitable in a situation of this kind, the Soviet union has rushed in to exploit it. I read in the press the other day that not only have they showed their sympathy with Iceland in this dispute, but that they have offered Soviet credits to help build an Icelandic trawler fleet which would be of great help to Iceland in the same way as the Soviet offer to help buy the fishing output of Iceland has been of help to her.
It would be a tragedy, I think, if anything developed which would force Iceland out of NATO, and we must all hope that nothing of that kind will happen. I appreciate the British difficulties in this regard, because this is a very important matter to them in view of the value of this fishing ground, but the situation has been made even more difficult for Britain by the fact that the Soviet union has for many years-perhaps going back as far as the establishment of the Soviet state; I am not sure-maintained its claim to a 12-mile territorial water zone. There has been no effort on anybody's part, as far as I know, to challenge that claim. Hon. members will therefore be able to appreciate the difficulty in which the United Kingdom government is placed.
I am suggesting, before we call it one o'clock, that because of our very close relationship to Iceland-I have been there myself and talked to the government and the people, and I think it is true to say that there is no country with which Iceland has a closer relationship than Canada

having regard to that fact and, perhaps, to our even closer relationship with the mother country, perhaps this is a situation in which Canada could offer her good offices for mediation which could be helpful in this case and prevent this dispute coming to a clash.
We must all hope that nothing like this will happen, but some of the reports in the last few days have indicated that if something is not done we may be in serious trouble, not only inside NATO but in trouble which would affect the whole north Atlantic defense position of which Iceland is a key base.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
