Mr. Chairman, before lunch in commenting on the minister's interesting statement of this morning I had attempted to deal with some aspects of the crisis in the Middle East and had also ventured to bring to the attention of the committee an
Supply-External Affairs unfortunate and what might be a damaging dispute between the United Kingdom on the one hand and Iceland on the other concerning the jurisdiction of Iceland over the 12-mile limit which she now claims and which conflicts with the United Kingdom law and practice in this field of territorial waters. I expressed the hope and I repeat it now that perhaps the good offices of the Canadian government might be useful in this matter in preventing this dispute which has been a long standing one and which came up in NATO over two years ago from deteriorating, and which will help to prove the reports of impending trouble to be without validity.
I was going on from there to discuss what is probably as important an aspect of our foreign relations as there is, our relations with the United States of America. One element in that relationship is our desire to co-operate with the United States in all aspects of foreign policy including policy in the Far East. I mention this matter which before one o'clock I did not intend to raise because of reports which have come over the air during the luncheon recess and which the minister may have heard to the effect that thousands of shells are being thrown on the little island of Quemoy and Matsu off the China mainland by the Chinese communist forces. There is some anxiety that this might be the prelude to an attack on these two islands which are now occupied by the government of Chiang Kai-shek and which are so close to the mainland of China which is under communist control that they have for several years constituted a threat to peace and stability in that area.
The secretary of state of the United States is reported as having said this morning that if this action should be the prelude to an effort on the part of the Chinese communist government to take and occupy these two offshore islands that would create a dangerous situation and, if I may quote from the words attributed to him, "Any such action." said Mr. Dulles, "would be a threat to the peace of the area." Indeed, this is the attitude that was adopted by the United States and expressed as such some time ago when there was a threat to these islands. I shall not quote his exact words but certainly the burden of his remarks at that time which are reported to have been repeated today was that those concerned could not count on the United States remaining aloof from an attack.
This does involve problems of peace and security in the area with which we are all concerned. I can only express the hope that no such development as has been indicated in this report will occur but if it does I think we in this house should know where the Canadian government stands in the matter.

Supply-External Affairs Perhaps, as an indication of the position adopted by the previous government and which I should like to confirm at this time as being the position which I think should be adopted in this matter by Canada, I may quote from Hansard of Tuesday, March 29, 1955, where at page 2477 the then private hon. member for Prince Albert who is now the Prime Minister asked me in my capacity as the then secretary of state for external affairs a question in these terms:
Is there any foundation for the general statement that is being made in the press of the United States that an imminent attack on Quemoy and Matsu by Red China is anticipated? Would the minister say whether he has any information that would confirm or deny this statement. Would he also give a general resume of the present situation relative to those two islands.
I replied to that question as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I have seen the reports to which my hon. friend refers and I have no information from any official quarter which would confirm them or that an attack on these islands is imminent.
I went on to say:
Of course, in the present situation it always remains a dangerous possibility.
Perhaps I may interpolate that it seems to remain a dangerous possibility at this moment. I then concluded my reply by saying as an indication of the policy we had adopted at that time and on which the minister might care to comment during the course of this debate:
As far as our policy-
That is, Canadian policy.
-in respect to this matter is concerned it has already been made clear, and I do not think I need repeat it here, that if an attack were made on these offshore islands it would not involve the intervention of the Canadian government.
That seems to me to be the right position for Canada to adopt in respect of this matter. In that sense it separates us to an important extent from the position that has been adopted and, according to reports, repeated by the secretary of state of the United States today. In so far as this represents a difference in policy between the two countries that is unfortunate. I think all hon. members of this committee and all Canadians desire to keep to a minimum these differences between the two countries that share this continent but there are times when we may have to differ with the United States and in respect of the attitude toward these offshore islands which has once again been very forcefully brought to our attention this seems to me to be such an occasion.
This brings me then to the more general subject of our relations with the United States. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, those relationships should be as close and friendly as possible. We should consider it a privilege

in this country as they should across the line to co-operate with each other in the economic defence and all other phases of foreign policy. I said in this house as recently as July 18, and I repeat it now because it is something that has been misinterpreted and I believe misconstrued, that there may not be between our two countries that close and continuous co-operation-and, yes, I might use the word "unity"-on defence matters which is desirable if we have economic conflicts.
That is why we must all be happy for reasons other than trade to take part in steps which may be taken to remove economic conflicts between the two countries, because those two things, economic conflict and defence co-operation, do not go together.
In this relationship between our two countries, any Canadian government, any Canadian representative, has to stand up for the rights of his own country as he conceives them, always having regard to what he can do to maintain unity inside the coalition and unity inside the continent which we all accept as essential. But that does not mean-in fact, it should never mean-that we should indulge in unfair criticism, unnecessary criticism, of the policies of our neighbour, that we should show an oversensitiveness, that we should go in for what you might call pinpricks, disturbing by small talk which sometimes causes the trouble that small talk can cause, disturbing the good relationship, the good day-to-day relationship which is essential.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, as an important aspect of our foreign policy I want to say something about the relationship between our two countries as I conceive it in the Arctic. A few days ago in this house one of the members on the treasury benches had some observations to make on this subject, in which he expressed chagrin and a sense of shame at some of the difficulties that Canadians were encountering, including members of the Canadian government, in their own north country, arising out of the fact there are United States facilities and installations in that part of Canada, which are there as a result of an agreement between Canada and the United States. When the Prime Minister cleared this matter up on August 16, he said, as reported at page 3652 of Hansard:
I have felt that in the northern defences of Canada there were in existence situations that could conceivably derogate from Canada's sovereignty.
Mr. Chairman, it is important that there should not be situations which derogate from our sovereignty in this part of Canada, and

if those situations arise out of the arrangements which were made between the Canadian and the United States governments for the construction of defence facilities in that part of Canada, more particularly the D.E.W. line, then I think it is desirable, and I think it will be wise, to put on the record in Hansard the agreement, or some parts of the agreement reached between our two countries for the establishment of the distant early warning system. This agreement was effected by an exchange of notes, which were signed at Washington on May 5, 1955. Under that agreement, Mr. Chairman-and it would certainly be unfortunate if it were otherwise-it seems to me that there is complete and necessary protection of the Canadian sovereign rights in the areas which are concerned, namely the Artie areas, where the D.E.W. line would be established. In the annex to the exchange of notes the arrangements are given which I think are pretty adequate for the protection of those rights of sovereignty. For instance, in paragraph 1 of the annex under the heading of "Sites" there is this:
Canada will acquire and retain title to all lands required for the system.
That is the D.E.W. line system.
Canada grants and assures the United States, without charge, such rights as access, use, and occupancy as may be required for the construction, equipment and operation of the system.
Then, section 6, under the heading "Canadian law", we find this:
Nothing in this agreement shall derogate from the application of Canadian law in Canada, provided that,-
And this is a proviso which I think in all fairness 1 should read:
-if in unusual circumstances its application may lead to unreasonable delay or difficulty in construction or operation, the United States authorities concerned may request the assistance of Canadian authorities in seeking appropriate alleviation.
Then section 7, under "Operation and Manning" we have these words:
It is understood that, in any event, Canada reserves the right, on reasonable notice, to take over the operation and manning of any or all of the installations.
Then, again, in section 15, under the heading "Use of Airstrips" we have this:
The airstrip shall be available for use by the R.C.A.F. as required. The airstrip shall also be available for use by Canadian civil air carriers operating into or through the area, whenever such use would not conflict with military requirements,-
This is a reasonable condition. I continue:
-and subject to the understanding that the United States air force will not be responsible for the provision of accommodation, fuel, or servicing facilities of any kind. Proposals and arrangements for such use of U.S.A.F.-operated airstrips by Canadian
Supply-External Affairs
air carriers shall be submitted to the R.C.A.F., which shall consult the U.S.A.F. before granting any such permission.
Then, section 16 under "Landing Facilities":
Landing facilities at any of the stations on tidewater will be available for use by Canadian government ships and ships employed on Canadian government business.
Then, under section 20, "Status of Forces" there is this:
The "Agreement between the parties to the North Atlantic Treaty regarding the status of their forces", signed in London on June 19, 1951, shall apply.
That means, in a word, that the rights under that agreement, under that NATO agreement, to which the United States forces are entitled, are available to any Canadian forces that might be on United States territory. Then, section 21 has this to say:
Supplementary arrangements or administrative agreements between authorized agencies of the two governments may be made from time to time for the purpose of carrying out the intent of this agreement.
Mr. Chairman, this agreement which was signed in 1955 does seem to me to protect Canadian rights and Canadian sovereignty in that area. When the Prime Minister indicated that there had been, as he thought, some derogation from that sovereignty, I asked him whether he would table the regulations made under this agreement which, according to the Prime Minister, cleared up those difficulties and were undoubtedly made under section 21, which I think-

Therefore it would be of great interest to the committee to ascertain the regulations which were passed since that time to clear up this situation. In any event, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the agreement in question does protect our sovereign rights and I also point out the fact, of which the Prime Minister

Supply-External Affairs undoutbedly is aware, that under the exchange of notes to which this document was attached, the Canadian government has full authority at any time to take over, to operate, to man and to maintain the D.E.W. line.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if this type of operation in the north is going to cause the kind of suspicion we sometimes see in the press and in other places, if there is going to be this kind of difficulty, if we feel, and I think it is a reasonable feeling, that it is necessary for us to increase our occupation of our own northern territories in order to establish beyond question our title to those territories by right of occupation, then perhaps the time is coming when Canada should exercise its option and take over, man and maintain the D.E.W. line, the weather stations and other Arctic installations now either jointly operated and maintained or operated and maintained by the United States.
There is now one reason and there may be more than one reason for so doing. Certainly there was some doubt when these installations were considered in the first place whether this would be a desirable thing for Canada to do. The construction of them involved great expense and it also involved the use of skilled manpower which perhaps was not available in Canada at that time. But if these difficulties have now been overcome, and they certainly have been so far as construction is concerned because construction is completed, and if there is now sufficient skilled manpower to take over the operation then I think serious consideration should be given to that action. I feel quite certain that the United States would welcome such action on our part. As I said in the last debate on external affairs, perhaps it is now at least worthy of consideration whether some of our obligations outside of Canada might not be reduced if that is necessary to make it possible for us to take over all these Arctic operations which are not only so important for defence but have a real value in the opening up and developing of the country for other purposes.
There is only one other matter I want to mention and I do so because the minister quite rightly had something to say about it this morning. I refer to the recent announcement, I think made yesterday, by the United States and the United Kingdom that under certain circumstances-there were some conditions attached to it-they would be willing to suspend nuclear tests for a period of one year. As I ventured to say in the house yesterday and as the Prime Minister emphasized in his statement, this was an important decision and it was an encouraging one as far as it went. It remains now, as the minister pointed out this morning, for those countries

which have in the past made these nuclear tests to get together as a result of the discussions now visualized in the United States and British statements, and try to come to some international agreement under the auspices of the United Nations, I would hope, which would formalize this important move on their part and perhaps extend it in terms of time and countries.
It is not only important that the three nuclear powers do this now but surely it is also important, as I have said before, that other powers which do not now manufacture nuclear weapons should associate themselves with this kind of agreement so that they will not in the future become manufacturers of nuclear weapons. Possibly at least the first step in that direction can be taken at the forthcoming assembly of the United Nations so that we not only can put an end to nuclear tests on the part of the powers which possess nuclear weapons of mass destruction but also can prevent the extension of the manufacture of these weapons to countries which do not now possess them.
When I advocate that I do not want to be misunderstood because I have at the same time suggested, and I repeat the statement now, that while the abolition not only of such tests but of nuclear weapons themselves is the first objective we should all seek there is a very great difference indeed between a megaton hydrogen bomb and a warhead for a ground to air defensive missile such as the Bomarc which cannot be used for any offensive purpose but which might be invaluable for defence against aggression. As soon as the warhead of the Bomarc is equipped with a nuclear tip it becomes a nuclear weapon, and as long as these tactical weapons for defence are used-I do not think this is inconsistent with the position I have taken regarding the abolition of nuclear tests- I think it is not a tolerable proposition that a Canadian squadron serving with a United States squadron on Canadian soil, perhaps under joint United States-Canadian command, should be armed in the future with Bomarc weapons without nuclear warheads while at the same time the United States squadron operating from the same field should have them.
That is why I ventured to ask the minister previously, and perhaps he may have something to say about this when he replies, whether any negotiations are under way in Washington now to put Canada on exactly the same basis of exchange with regard to nuclear weapons as the United Kingdom. I know that this requires an agreement under the United States atomic energy act, but I suggest that in the present situation and because of the close relationship we have

with the United States in defence such an agreement should be sought and that we should not be expected to work out our continental defence arrangements with the United States under a continental defence command with this difference as to weapons existing between us. I do not consider this inconsistent with my view on the abolition of nuclear weapons. So I hope that as long as this situation persists we will be put on a basis of equality with the United States so far as exchange of information and tactical defensive air weapons are concerned. Surely that is a reasonable request to make to the United States, and I cannot believe for a minute that they would refuse to make that kind of an arrangement with a country so close to them in so many ways if the approach is made to them.

We in this group, Mr. Chairman, welcome the Secretary of State for External Affairs on his return from the special assembly of the United Nations. Before proceeding further I might say that while we do not agree on some questions or on some details of policy, we wish him well in all he undertakes with a view to improving international understanding and obtaining international agreement in his efforts working towards international peace.
I listened with a great deal of interest to his report on the Arab resolution and the details surrounding it. I am not going to repeat his words or take the time of the committee to go into details. I must say that from our point of view it was a most interesting development and, I repeat, a most heartening one.
We in this group are glad that this was a unanimous vote and that it appears that the United States in this vote recognized the realities of the Arab situation and, shall I say, the peculiarities of the Arab situation and also to a great extent western world opinion, and also, in supporting this resolution, the responsibility of the United Nations for dealing with this problem over the long run.
Before proceeding I might say that it is well known that this group strongly opposes unilateral action on the part of any country in attempting to deal with a situation like this. I might say that we are not alone in Canada in that respect. Prominent Conservative papers, prominent Liberal papers, other prominent periodicals and a good number of prominent people that support all of the parties in this country or the various parties in this house have expressed opinions similar to ours in that respect.

I was very much interested in the minister's statement that there were deep divisions in the general assembly as to the value or function of an international police force. However, I was very pleased to hear him say that this matter is going to be given further study and consideration. We are very much interested in that aspect of the protective forces of the United Nations. In any event, Mr. Chairman, this unanimous support for the Arab resolution and the spirit that appeared to surround it creates great hope in all of us, I think, and offers a great opportunity to the United Nations, possibly the greatest opportunity it has had to deal with the basic problem that surrounds this Middle East situation that it has had for many years. It gives what I would call a breathing spell. It gives us a cause for cautious optimism.
We were all pleased to hear the minister's remarks with respect to the suspension of nuclear tests by the United Kingdom and the United States for a period of one year. This gives further cause for relief and gives another opportunity to go further and to try to get wider agreement even with other nations in the western world and we hope, finally, with the Soviet union.
I am sure we all feel that the minister was justified in feeling better over the international situation than he has at any time since he became a member of this house. I listened as usual with a great deal of interest to the Leader of the Opposition. We must all recognize the fact that with his knowledge and his long experience as secretary of state for external affairs he has a great advantage over a simple backwoodsman like myself. He knows the majority of the leading figures, and he possibly knows the physical features of most of the countries with which he has had to deal and on that account he would know the circumstances surrounding all these problems. I always listen to him with great interest, although I thought this afternoon that the text of his speech was rather pointless in some directions. I expected him to be a little more emphatic in some instances.
However, I and the other members of this group were very pleased to hear him speak of the need for building up an international police force. While we all recognize the difficulties, nations being what they are, I do not think we should ever lose sight of this objective that we should eventually replace regional and other pacts with an international police force having the authority to maintain world law and order. Other members of this group will have a few words to say on various aspects of this question, so I am not going to deal with it further at this time but will turn to other matters.

As a member of the committee on external affairs, I have had the opportunity to attend meetings of the committee again this session. I have found them to be of great interest and somewhat profitable. The estimates of this department total some $69,484,506, which sounds like a lot of money to many Canadians but I think we must realize first of all that approximately half of that amount goes for expenditures under the Colombo plan or grants to the various United Nations agencies. In reality, therefore, we spend, I would judge, about $35 million on the administration of the Department of External Affairs. That still sounds like a lot of money but, as I view them, our expenditures in this department have increased in ratio to the increase in Canada's responsibility in international affairs and I am sure that no one possessing a knowledge of the world situation today and the responsibilities which Canada must be willing to accept in respect of international affairs would begrudge $35 million out of a budget of over $6 billion as Canada's contribution to the furthering of international understanding and agreement. We in this group consider that our expenditures on external affairs are a first rate investment in the cause of understanding between nations.
The committee examined the estimates in detail and gathered a lot of information from the senior officials of the department and from General McNaughton, the chairman of the international joint commission. Before proceeding, I must say that the members of this group recognize, as I am sure other hon. members recognize, the high calibre and the devoted service of the officials of the Department of External Affairs. I, for one, have noticed since I have been a member of this house that with the expansion of the department there has been even an improvement, shall I say, in the calibre of many members of the staff, and naturally with the developments which have occurred during the last ten years there has been a much broader base of understanding of world problems and Canada's relationship thereto.
I would like to refer briefly to the report of the committee and to bring three or four matters to the attention of this committee, but before doing so I should express the appreciation of the members of that committee for the very fair way in which the chairman arranged sittings sometimes to meet the convenience of members who were sitting on other committees at the same time. We appreciated that consideration very much indeed.

Supply-External Affairs
The first paragraph of the report to which I would like to refer is the following:
The announcement by the Prime Minister of the preliminary step toward the establishment of a parliamentary committee to meet with a United States congressional committee, to examine problems common to both countries and to exchange views and interpret developments to their respective governments was welcomed by your committee. Such a joint committee, it is felt, could be invaluable in the promotion of a greater degree of understanding between the two legislative bodies.
I must say that we in this group give wholehearted support to that opinion of the committee because we believe that not only would it promote a greater understanding between the two legislative bodies but that a committee of this sort, if it is established and is permitted to function regularly and continually, will do a great deal to promote a better understanding on the part of United States legislators and the people of the United States with respect to the particular problems which concern us in Canada. I do hope that the Prime Minister will make arrangements for the establishment of that committee at the earliest possible date, at least so far as this parliament is concerned.
The next paragraph to which I would like to refer is the following:
With regard to the recent report of the United Nations scientific committee on the effect of atomic radiation, your committee expresses a hope that the government will keep under constant review its policy on the suspension of nuclear tests, taking into account the results of the current meetings of scientists at Geneva on the methods of detecting nuclear explosions.
We all heard the very welcome announcement made by the Prime Minister yesterday, since this report was drafted, with respect to the suspension of nuclear tests for one year by agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States. That is a step in the right direction but this paragraph was inserted in the report as a reflection of the committee's concern with respect to this problem and its anxiety that the government should keep under constant review its policy on the suspension of these tests.
The third paragraph to which I wish to draw the attention of the committee reads as follows:
The continuation of studies on the possible establishment of a permanent United Nations force to ensure peace and deter aggression, is considered of great importance.
I might say that the committee's report was adopted unanimously, so that that is an expression of the opinion of all members of the committee. We do hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will strongly support the final necessity for some form of United Nations police force coming into being.
[Mr. Herridge.l
We know the road will be a difficult, rocky and slow one, but we feel that we should not lose sight of this objective. The final paragraph of the committee's report, which I believe is very interesting, is as follows:
In order to assist your committee in its work, it recommends that, at future sessions of parliament it should commence its sittings within one month of the meeting of the house. Consideration should also be given to the broadening of the role of the committee.
It is those last words in which I am particularly interested "the broadening of the role of the committee". That recommendation indicates a certain feeling on the part of committee members, regardless of party, that the committee could perform a greater function rather than being entirely limited to examination of estimates and the questioning of officials. While such activities are very useful and very necessary the committee members felt that the government should give consideration to the broadening of the role of the committee. While the government is responsible for policy, we do feel that the committee could serve an even more- useful purpose by having certain problems referred to it, maybe problems of a technical nature such as the testing of nuclear weapons, or the problems surrounding disarmament and other matters which might arise as a result of immediate situations. We feel the role of the committee could be extended to the great advantage of this House of Commons in general while, as I have said before, the government accepts the responsibility for policy on external affairs. That is why the committee unanimously adopted that last recommendation in its report.
Mr. Chairman, I see that the Prime Minister is looking this way and I am sure he will be interested to hear what is the foreign policy of the C.C.F. party. We held a national convention on April 23, 24 and 25 in Montreal attended by several hundred delegates from all across Canada. Those delegates had given consideration at the local level to the question of a foreign policy for Canada. The resolutions on foreign policy which were brought to the convention in abundance, were thoroughly discussed for a period of one day and finally sublimated, if I may use that word, in one resolution which was accepted by the convention and adopted. I wish to place on record what the foreign policy of the C.C.F. is at the present time. I will read the resolution and make a comment or two on it.
Foreign Policy
The race between the United States and the Soviet union to achieve superiority in the production and stockpiling of nuclear and thermo-nuclear weapons is creating a fearful atmosphere throughout the world. New and more powerful weapons, with

a capacity to destroy that confounds the imagination, are being developed at an alarming rate. The C.C.F. warns that this situation cannot continue without a great risk of a world conflagration that could lead to the extinction of life on this planet.
Since that preamble was included in that resolution the Prime Minister has made an announcement which is a heartening step in the right direction.
Believing that it is urgent that greater emphasis be placed on positive means to ease international tensions and further the cause of peace, the convention urges:
1.	That the testing of nuclear weapons be immediately abandoned and banned by all countries.
We hope we are all working toward that end.
2.	That distribution of nuclear weapons to NATO and Warsaw pact countries be discontinued.
Very strong emphasis was placed on that point at our national conference.
3.	That as soon as the testing and distribution of nuclear weapons has been stopped, a concerted effort be made to move forward to a policy of progressive disarmament involving both nuclear and conventional weapons, subject to adequate international inspection and control through the United Nations.
We in this group hope that events in recent days have provided some further opportunity for developments in that direction.
4.	That advantage be taken of every opportunity for negotiation between the western powers and the U.S.S.R. with a view to establishing a neutralized zone in central Europe, and finding a solution to other political problems.
Though on account of recent events our eyes have been directed to the Middle East, we still have the core of the international situation situated, as it were, in the heart of Europe. For that reason the C.C.F. included that paragraph in its foreign policy declaration.
We also urge:
5.	That a permanent international police force be established under the United Nations for use in critical situations as the occasion arises.
I made a few remarks on that subject earlier.
6.	That, pending a large general settlement between eastern and western powers which will make it possible to dispense with regional alliances such as NATO, every policy be promoted which strengthens economic co-operation among NATO countries.
I do not think anyone would fail to recognize the fact that we have done very little to date to give effect to article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty.
7.	That much greater emphasis be placed on economic aid through the United Nations, and to this end Canada should offer to contribute at least one per cent of its national income to a world plan of economic aid and development.
We have taken some steps in that direction, but we in this group believe we could do more and should do more. And finally:
Supply-External Affairs
The C.C.F. believes that Canada, in advancing these policies, should seek at all times to develop her own foreign policy and not allow herself to become compromised by views abroad which do not effectively promote world peace.
On that point, Mr. Chairman, I want to say on behalf of this group that while we realize there has been some progress we should like to see this government speak with a stronger voice on certain issues. We notice that the courage of our government is in ratio, shall I say, to the settlement of any international situation; we wait for other governments to act; we become brave after the problem has been met by the announcements of governments of greater nations. We do urge the government to speak with a stronger voice as far as Canada is concerned, and to use its prestige and influence in the world to give a lead on important issues and to indicate that Canada has a foreign policy which is not entirely dependent on Mr. Dulles or anybody of his mind.
We believe this could be done by standing up at this time and giving recognition to the government of China. When we find people like Mr. Muir going over there, to investigate conditions and when the Royal Bank of Canada prints his address in its monthly pamphlet entitled: "The Challenge of China"; when we find industrialists in British Columbia, large mining and smelting concerns and leaders of other industries in British Columbia, urging this action, then surely the government must realize that such a move would receive the support of the vast majority of the Canadian people.
We urge the government of Canada to take this step and show we are not waiting for the United States to take action first. The United States will recognize China at some future time, and if our government continues its present policy we can look forward to the recognition of China the day after the United States does so. We ask this government to take the lead.
To indicate British opinion on this matter I want to quote from a very reputable paper, the Christian Science Monitor of August 15, 1958. The article is headed "Bevan Rips Dulles on Red China Snub", and this is what Mr. Bevan, as reported in this newspaper, had to say:
If they persist in their present policies, then the smaller powers should concert among themselves to defy a leadership so myopic, so smugly self-satisfied, so dangerous and so unequal to the imperious needs of the times.
The article goes on:
Unfortunately for the smooth-running of Anglo-American relations, the majority of British people agree with Mr. Bevan in his deploring of American non-recognition of communist China.
It is one of the very few matters of which the nation as a whole does agree with Mr. Bevan.

Supply-External Affairs
I urge on behalf of this group that the government indicate that we do have an independent foreign policy. Let the government speak with a strong voice for Canada and recognize the government of China; let it speak with a stronger voice for the development of international agreement for the abandonment of nuclear tests; let it speak with a stronger voice in drawing attention to the economic injustice suffered by multitudes of people, because we know that there can be no peace in the world until economic injustice is removed from the Middle East, or from the Far East, or wherever it is found. And let it speak with a stronger voice with respect to the need for speeding up negotiations on disarmament as a result of an international agreement on inspection.
In conclusion I may say that the contribution of this group to the debate is a plea to the government of Canada to speak up with a stronger voice on the subjects I have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, now
that the government has 50 Quebec members to support it in this house, and that these gentlemen have no doubt acquired some sense of responsibility since the last elections, I hope that they will side with their government in respect of the Colombo plan and of the help to be given to under-developed countries. I hope that we will be spared this myth which was circulated in recent election campaigns, a myth fostered by reactionaries more concerned with demagogic advantage than with finding a solution to the great problems with which humanity is faced at this time.
Mr. Chairman, those of us who sit on this side of the house are proud to see that this year the government has increased assistance to under-developed countries under the Colombo plan. I do not think there is any greater challenge to western countries than to help raise the living standards of those countries situated along the borders of Russia and China and whose political organization has been developing along democratic lines.
I have the feeling that, at times, our political analysts and commentators overemphasize the few errors that Canada has possibly made in the international field; for they were errors made in good faith. On the other hand, I believe our successes are being underplayed. Indeed I do not know of anything we could have done that has been more practical, more human, and more likely to bring dividends than the assistance we have been giving for the last two years under the Colombo Plan. And the Liberals are very proud of their leadership in that regard because those countries badly need that assistance.

In the whole history of mankind, I do not know of any similar example, or precedent, where countries, for the sake of the survival of democracy on earth, shared their surpluses with needy nations. And we are not the poorer for it; we are as rich as we were a few years ago. Yet if, so far, we have been favoured and protected by providence, it is true that, even in Canada, people have, from time to time, to face hardship, and I know of none more cruel than that which has been visited upon us since March 31st last. However, Mr. Chairman, we are quite resigned to it, knowing that it is only temporary.

Mr. Chairman, on this item, which is a further item for departmental administration, I want to raise a particular matter. During this session all members in this house have expressed their concern regarding, and their unaltered opposition to, the Soviet union whenever it has done something that we felt should rightly be condemned, and in the case of Imre Nagy it was said in all parts of this house that his execution was an international tragedy. I think it is our duty to raise anything that we feel is wrong and should not take place, and perhaps more particularly if this possible occurrence should be within the boundaries of a friendly nation. I think Canadians in all walks of life have been deeply disturbed by the report of the pending execution, because of a sentence in the courts of Alabama, of a man by the name of Jimmie Wilson for having stolen $1.95 from a white woman.
In our discussion of external affairs it is possible for members in this house to refer to actions in any other nation of the world even though, as is always the case, we have no direct control and no direct responsibility

Supply-External Affairs over what may happen. The nation to the south of us is a friendly nation, a nation of people with whom we get along exceedingly well and a nation which has a particular place in my own heart because my mother happened to be born in the United States and did not come to Canada until she was an adult woman. I may say that my early recollections of discussions in our home as to the relative advantage of the Canadian type of parliamentary constitution and the United States type I had it impressed upon me very vigorously by my mother that the United States system in some particulars had some very distinct advantages. Therefore, I am not in any way anti-United States; if anything, I am pro-United States. Because of that, it disturbs me even more to think that under their law such a sentence may be carried out, and within the next few days.
As I understand it, the jurisdiction over clemency is under the governor of the state of Alabama, James E. Folsom. I have read reports-in fact, I have them in front of me-saying that the governor of that state very frequently has taken a lenient and humanitarian approach to such problems. I would express the hope that in this case the lenient, humanitarian aspects of the governor's character would prevail and that this execution may be prevented and will not take place.
President Eisenhower of the United States has taken a very stalwart attitude in opposition to discrimination within his nation because of race, colour or creed. Parliamentarians in all parties in Canada take that same attitude. I express the hope in the parliament of Canada that humanitarian aspects and attitudes and the deep generosity of the United States people will prevail and that this execution will not take place. I have said that I make this request on humanitarian grounds. There are other grounds. I think it would be an international calamity if the leaders of the communist world were given this ready-made club with which to continue their nefarious and troublesome course in the world.
I am not asking the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make a public pronouncement. I am not even asking him to say whether the Canadian government has given any thought to the matter but as a fellow member of parliament I do say to him that it is my hope that he and the government will use what I believe to be Canada's very great influence at all levels in the United States to see if we can assist in preventing this very disastrous thing from taking place on September 5.

I do not want to enter into a general discussion of a matter concerning another country, for gratuitous advice coming from this country respecting the administration of the criminal law of another country would be improper. In his opening words the hon. member referred to the strong stand taken when the premier of Hungary was murdered, in a totally tyrannical and unjustified manner. I do not take second place to anybody in humanitarian feelings respecting the need in these days of the rigours of the criminal law not being applied in the manner in which they were a little more than 100 years ago, but it would indeed be most improper for this government to take any action along the lines suggested, although not directly requested, by the hon. gentleman.
As I understand it, under the law of Alabama robbery is an offence punishable with death, and the fact that the convicted man is of one colour or another does not enter into the equation. I can still remember one of my forebears, who lived not to such a great age, telling me as a boy of executions taking place in what is now this province for the theft of two or three shillings. The general trend in all countries has been towards amelioration of the terrible penalties that used to be imposed, and having regard to the situation in the case in question and the fact that there is the right of appeal available to the state supreme court, in addition to the right of commutation of sentence in the governor, I am sure that the fears of the hon. gentleman may well be expected to be dissolved in the light of the reaction of the people within that country without other countries making known their views, based on the deep and abiding necessity of assuring the humanitarian ideals and emotions that move us all.

I have just one word to say on the matter raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia. If and when one incident violates or appears to violate principles of law and justice, whether in our own country or in a neighbouring and friendly country, if and when that happens we do harm to ourselves and we do harm to the principles which we proclaim. Those systems which are not founded on our concept of law and justice seize on such violations and magnify and distort them in a way that harms the cause of freedom and free people everywhere.
I do not know all the facts in this particular case. If they are as reported in the press it would appear to be a tragic matter. But the United States, our friendly neighbour, is a land of law and justice, a land where people can right wrongs and correct

injustices, and if there is wrong or injustice in this case I have confidence that the people of that state and that country will correct it.

speechtext: I thank the Leader of the Opposition for his contribution to this discussion. I trust that the hope expressed by the Prime Minister in the concluding words of his statement will be borne out in subsequent days. The Prime Minister has said that the sentence imposed under the law of the state of Alabama is based entirely on a conviction for robbery and that colour has nothing to do with it whatsoever. That may be a correct statement of the written law but I am fearful, as I think many informed people are, that the application of the law is much more severe and rigorous in the case of a coloured man who is found guilty of robbing a white woman than in a similar case if a white person is found guilty. I am certain that a great many thinking people would question the assumption made by the Prime Minister but even if he were correct it is just as regrettable that this conviction should be hanging over a man who, according to the reports we read, has been found guilty of an offence involving the stealing of $1.95.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it occurred to me that in the interests of orderly discussion it might be well if I made a few remarks on the first division in these estimates, namely the citizenship registration branch and the citizenship branch, and reserved any further comments which I might make on immigration or on Indian affairs to their respective divisions.

I wonder whether the hon. lady would permit me to intervene. I think it has always been customary, on the departmental administration item which is the item which has been called, to permit a certain amount of general discussion. Of course 57071-3-255
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I would not want to usurp the place of the hon. lady if she wished to go first on that item, but I think it might help, as it might possibly be unnecessary to have much discussion on the other items if we had a rather general discussion on the first item.

I think the hon. member misunderstood me. I intend to make a few remarks here on the citizenship registration branch and the citizenship branch but anything further that is to be said on immigration or on Indian affairs I propose to deal with on votes 62 and 66 respectively.
The Canadian citizenship registration branch is charged, as hon. members know, with the determination of the status of persons claiming Canadian citizenship, the examination of applications under the act of persons applying for Canadian citizenship and the preparation of certificates. The branch is also responsible for the procedures involving revocation or loss of Canadian citizenship and the procedures pertaining to the registration of births of Canadian citizens outside of Canada.
During 1957 more than 151,000 applications under the Canadian Citizenship Act were received by the branch compared with approximately 100,000 in 1956. As a result of these applications approximately 142,000 certificates were prepared, 95,000 of which were granted to persons acquiring Canadian citizenship in 1957. In 1956 a total of almost 80,000 certificates were prepared, 55,000 of which were granted to applicants for citizenship. Citizenship was granted in 1957 to 8,650 British subjects, and 86,812 aliens, while in 1956, 5,812 British subjects and 49,590 aliens were granted Canadian citizenship. There were more than 39,000 miniature certificates issued during 1957. This is an increase of more than 21,000 over 1956.
In this connection I should like to refer to remarks made early this session by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville, and I quote from page 15 of the English translation of the speech he delivered in French on May 26, 1958:
It is a well known and incontrovertible fact that, at this time, Canadian citizens are unable to produce an efficient means of identification. Yet everybody knows that the introduction of legislation designed to remedy this situation would be highly advantageous.
Then later in his speech he went on to say this:
What does the Canadian citizen have today by way of identification? We have nothing but secondary documents: a driver's licence, a pass, a credit card, all of which can be stolen by someone else and used fraudulently. In my opinion, it is absolutely necessary that people have a real identification card, so made that it could not be imitated.

The hon. member submitted that this responsibility should be entrusted to the Department ot Citizenship and Immigration. It is unfortunate that the hon. member did not take time to check his facts. Had he done so, he would have learned that since October 1954 the Canadian citizenship registration branch of this department has been issuing pocket size certificates of citizenship laminated in plastic, carrying a photograph and a specimen signature of the bearer, together with pertinent descriptive information. Since October 1954, more than 65,000 of these miniature certificates have been issued to Canadian citizens and the demand for them is greater each year.
As the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville apparently needs a proper identification document, if he will fill in the appropriate form which he can obtain from my office, and return it accompanied by two photographs of himself, I will see that he gets a miniature citizenship certificate, without payment of the regular fee, as a gift from the minister.
To return to registration, 86 per cent of the applicants for citizenship in 1957 resided in urban areas, while 14 per cent resided in rural districts. For applicants in rural areas residing some distance from a court special procedures are available under the act, whereby they may file their applications directly with the registrar. In order to deal with these applications from remote areas, 24 persons were appointed under the Canadian Citizenship Act in 1957 to act as courts for citizenship purposes. These apointments brought to 65 the number of courts so appointed.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by pointing out to the committee or, perhaps I should say, reminding those members of the committee who were in a similar committee in the last brief parliament that when the hon. lady presented the estimates of another department at that time I predicted that she would soon advance in the cabinet. My prediction turns out to have been right. The hon. lady began her career as minister by occupying the portfolio that was entrusted to me when I began my career as minister. She has now succeeded to the other portfolio I held while I was a minister. The highest hope I can express for the hon. lady is that after the next election she may find herself where I am now.
That is not much of a hope.

Of course, it may well be that in spite of that I will do what I can before that time comes to see that the hon.


lady is not even here at all. However, that is not meant to be a threat. I think there are other ministers whom I would sooner take on in verbal combat than the hon. lady because I imagine she could rally to her support quite considerable numbers not only of the members of her own sex but perhaps even more of the other.
I want to say that it has been my view- and I was rather proud of this fact when I occupied the position which the hon. lady now occupies-that this department, namely the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, through its activities has contributed greatly to that quite extraordinary development of our country that has taken place in the years since immigration was resumed after the second world war. I must say that I very much appreciated a tribute that was paid the other day to what had happened to this country in those years, so much so that I should like to recall to the minds of members of the committee this statement:
Canada's future promises tremendous expansion and, in my opinion, greater than any other nation in the world in the next quarter century.
Those words I wish particularly to commend to the committee.
Behind us is a record of nation-building unmatched in history;
That tribute to the work of the St. Laurent government by the present Prime Minister when he opened the exhibition in Toronto two days ago is very much appreciated on this side of the house.
Hear, hear.

I do think that the work of the hon. lady's department has greatly contributed to this end, but I must say I was not able to find quite the same encouragement in another part of the Prime Minister's speech on that occasion, when he said the following:
The employment situation is improving and in July 1958, Canadians with jobs numbered 5,934,000-
Mark these words:
-only 15,000 below the high level in 1957, and 145,000 more than in July 1956. There has been an upturn in employment this spring and summer-a good deal more than seasonal.
I think we can take only very limited satisfaction from these statistics. We have half a million more people in this country than we had when the present administration came into office and it is not much of a boast for the Prime Minister to make, that there are 15,000 fewer of them working. I have no doubt, of course, that that is the reason why the department is continuing to follow the policy which was the first change in policy from that followed by the previous

administration, the policy of severely restricted immigration. I am afraid it is very unlikely that if things go on the way they are going now the hon. lady will be able to boast, when she comes to the end of her career as minister of immigration, that she brought immigration to the highest point which had been reached since 1913, which was the record of the Liberal government.
Nothing I have heard during this parliament has moved me more than the words used by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort in his maiden speech in this house, and I make no apology for trespassing for a moment on the time of the committee to recall a few of those words at this time because they are strictly relevant to the work of the hon. lady's department. The hon. member talked about his arrival in Ottawa, and as reported at page 476 of Hansard for May 26, 1958, he said:
When I arrived here in Ottawa for the first time and walked across from Union station to parliament hill I was all eyes, and my heart was filled with emotion when I saw the graceful parliament buildings, the statues and the other historic sites. The first statue that I walked up to was that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the great French-Canadian statesman, and as I looked up I could almost see a twinkle in his eyes. I thought I could hear him say these words: "What are you, a little immigrant of just 29 years residence, here in Ottawa for? Didn't I hear you say that all you wanted from life was to come to Canada and to make a home for yourself and your family? I thought you were very content when Canada had given you this opportunity and your life's ambition was achieved, but now I see you are here as the new member for Humboldt-Melfort to represent this great constituency in the 24th parliament. As this is the case, go on then, and do the job assigned to you for the glory of Canada and your constituency." These are the words I thought I heard this great statesman say to me, and as I walked slowly away a vision appeared before my eyes depicting the last 29 years spent in this wonderful country of my adoption,
I do not think even the most stonyhearted of us could help but be moved by that statement. In the world in which we are now living there are very few countries about which such words could be used, and I am not seeking to make any particular point of this. I could not help but think that it was a good thing that the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort came to Canada in 1929, when the government was a Liberal government, because in 1930 the doors were closed and in the years after, from 1930 until 1935, we actually had a net emigration from this country. It does seem to me, sir, that this was one of those bad turns which we have taken in the course of our development, and I do hope we are not going to take another one now.
I am not suggesting, of course, that we have taken such a turn; I do not blame the present administration for not bringing to 57071-3-255J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Canada people who cannot find any work here. The position we took when in office and the position I would take if I were still in office is that it would be a great mistake -the greatest mistake we could possibly make so far as the future of immigration is concerned-if we encouraged people to come here to settle in this country when there were no opportunities for them to get jobs fairly quickly. My experience as a minister, and I am sure this is the experience of the hon. lady, is that one dissatisfied immigrant can do more harm to Canada's reputation abroad than one hundred do good. We cannot, of course, help having a few dissatisfied people, but we certainly do not want to bring immigrants to this country to be dissatisfied. I have no criticism of the fact, in itself, that at the present time because of limited employment opportunities the department is not bringing people here.
I do hope, and we all hope, that the conditions now prevailing will soon change and that the Prime Minister was right when he said there has been an upturn in employment this spring and summer, "a good deal more than seasonal". No one will rejoice at this more than those of us who believe that there is a great future in this country and that there is going to be room in it for even more people than those we can produce at home, and there is no reason for not producing at home all we reasonably can produce. My thoughts on that subject are very well known and I have never made any apology for them.
I was very pleased indeed when the hon. lady's department announced the other day that, in order to complete the liquidation of the situation created in the free world by the tragic events two years ago in Hungary, the Canadian government had undertaken to receive, if I remember the figure correctly, 1,100 more Hungarian refugees. On the day I read that announcement I asked a question in this house and was given some information which I do not have at hand but which is of the most encouraging and reassuring nature. I am sure that most Canadians will agree with these remarks if they are possessed of any breadth of view at all.
Here were people who had left their country with nothing but what they were wearing and who could not go back to their country for fear at least of imprisonment and possibly of death, who had none of the advantages of most immigrants but who, after one and a half years in Canada at the most, had made their way to such an extent that of the 35,000 who came here less than 1,000 were receiving support from the department. As a matter of fact I think the figure was a great deal less than that. Those who had thrown up

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the sponge and had gone back to Hungary numbered less than 500. I apologize for quoting these figures from memory, but I do not think my recollection is very far out and, if anything, I have given a high figure for those receiving assistance. What this means is that these people who had no intention or thought of ever coming to Canada until these tragic events took place, had made no preparation for what they would find here. Let us not forget that most of them were young people who lived for 15 years under a communist regime with all that that implies, are for the most part adapting themselves to the new and difficult conditions of a new country, establishing themselves, and that most of them are already self-supporting.
I would think that that is something in which we can take some satisfaction. I make no apology for saying that I am not ashamed of my part in it, and I want to say without any hesitation whatsoever that I am very appreciative of the fact that the present administration under the hon. lady and under the Minister of Justice who preceded her in charge of the department have followed precisely the policies that were followed by the previous administration, and that there has been no political controversy whatsoever about this very important migration.
Perhaps I might not have said this if we were not following immediately after the consideration of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, but I want to say that 3 believe that if the Canadian government, with the unanimous support of the Canadian parliament, had not shown the vigour which we showed in December of 1956, this problem of the free world would not have been solved. We Canadians did far more in relation to our size and resources than any other country in the world. In fact we have taken almost as many Hungarian refugees as the United States which has ten times our population and much more than ten times our wealth, and if we had not done what we did in the way we did it and with the vigour with which it was done-I am not seeking any special credit for myself, because we were all unanimous about it-this problem might not have been solved; and if tens of thousands of these Hungarians had gone back behind the iron curtain the moral effect on the whole world is something I should not like to be contemplating now. Therefore, I think we, as Canadians, regardless of party, can take some satisfaction in this one particular achievement of the hon. lady's department.
I have no other general observations to make at this stage about immigration but I do want to say one very brief word about citizenship, and only one very brief word at

this time. I noticed the other day-in fact, on June 30-a report in the Toronto Star of a meeting of the Czechoslovak Canadians in Toronto which was addressed by a predecessor of the hon. lady and of myself, the first minister of citizenship and immigration in the history of Canada, Hon. Walter Harris. During this meeting, Mr. Harris took exception to statements which had been made by one of the county judges. I am not going to give his name or the part of the country from which he comes because I have no desire to pillory anyone; it is just the sentiment that was expressed to which I want to take exception here, as Mr. Harris took exception to it on that occasion. This judge was reported to have said that many new Canadians are unwilling to renounce their countries of origin, and cited instances of Russian Canadians and Dutch Canadians turning out in national costume to greet visiting fellow countrymen. Mr. Harris' comment on this, which I want to make my own, was as follows:
I disagree with the judge. It is a proper thing to honour the visiting head of an allied state. If there was a free president of the state of Czechoslovakia I would expect you to honour him if he visited Canada.
Mr. Harris went on to point out that there was no need to lose one's pride in one's origin and to lose one's pride in one's heritage and one's past because one has become a Canadian citizen.
It seems to me that one of the reasons we have for having a greater pride in our citizenship than almost any other people in the world is that to as great an extent as any other country in the world, once we have admitted people to this country we do generally accept them, as fellow citizens on a basis of equality and I hope that may always be the case.
I want also to say a word, before I conclude these remarks, about the future of those original inhabitants of this country who were here before any of our ancestors or any of us came to this country. I feel, and I have always felt, that the supreme responsibility of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration-the most important responsibility of all -is that responsibility which appertains to another office which the hon. lady holds, the office of superintendent general of Indian affairs, which is the oldest office in the public service of Canada, an office which, like some of our ancestors, was transported across the Niagara river from the state of New York into Canada after the American revolution, an office which has persisted ever since.
It does seem to me that it should be our ambition in Canada to make that office obsolete, and that the supreme duty of anyone

charged with the responsibility for Indian affairs should be to see that the day will come as soon as possible when there will no longer be any Indian affairs in Canada, but not in the way, of course, in which that, unhappily, happened in the province in which I was elected.
We do know, of course, that in the last generation the Indian population of this country, far from decreasing as had been the case for a long time, has been increasing and that today it is increasing more rapidly than the rest of the population though it has no additions through immigration. We do know that the policy of segregation, whatever there may have been to say for it when it was adopted a century ago, is certainly no answer to the problem as it exists today. Not that anybody, least of all the superintendent general, should ever think of forcible desegregation, because there are so many of the Indians who fear that, as the minister has no doubt discovered and as I discovered on more than one occasion. But I do think it should be our aim to the greatest possible extent that it can be done by voluntary means and by persuasion to encourage, support and help the Indians to move away from segregation and to become ordinary members of the Canadian community.
Of course, I believe that the most effective way to achieve that, as soon as it can be done in an ordinary fashion without outraging people's feelings and without upsetting existing arrangements to which people have devoted their lives and energies until something better can replace them, would be to end segregation in education, and I hope the hon. lady, even if we are at the stage of trying to end the session as soon as we can and we do not want to take undue time on the estimates of her department, will tell us what progress is being made in the field of joint education.
By that I mean an arrangement for bringing the Indians into the same schools as other citizens so that they are brought up together from the beginning because there is no substitute for that, none whatever. I know a great many improvements have been made in the last ten years in the field of Indian education. Every year some new improvements are made. I do not expect the hon. lady has had very much time since she assumed her portfolio, and she has been sitting in the house most of the time since then, to make any great reforms herself but I would be interested if she would tell us what progress is being made particularly with the scholarship scheme that was instituted a year or two ago and what progress is being made in having more and more
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indians take vocational training and in encouraging some of the most promising of them to go to the universities.
There is another aspect of Indian integration which was very close to my heart when I was the minister and that is what was called economic development. Since the minister was not present last January when I last discussed the subject I shall make no apology for repeating very briefly what I said then about the useful things that were being done in this field. I remember the first time an approach was made to the gold mines to persuade them to take some Indians into their employ. I was approached by a representative of the mining association to see if I would not try to find immigrants to go into the mines. In reply I said, "You have labour right at your door, labour that has always been here. Will you not try Indians?" I must say that when I first suggested it the suggestion was considered startling. They seemed almost horrified at the idea but I persuaded them to make an attempt and I was greatly gratified by the reports I received of those experiences. I was also greatly pleased by the last report I heard of what was being done, particularly at Pickle Crow. I daresay the hon. lady may not herself have become familiar with that yet, but it is one of the more successful attempts to find really useful employment for the Indians in the area in which they live, a locality where perhaps it would not be too easy to persuade newcomers to the country to go in the first instance.
At the time I was in the department and in direct touch with this work we had a gentleman, Mr. Mel Jack, who has now moved on to other fields. I make no apology for mentioning his name. I had a little something to do with Mr. Jack coming into the department in the first place. I thought he brought to this work an imagination, an energy and sometimes an unorthodox approach that was not characteristic of all civil servants. Perhaps he was more the kind of civil servant I was than some other civil servants are but-
You are too modest.

-but I will not carry that analogy any further. What I am concerned about and my reason for mentioning this is that I want to be assured that the work Mr. Jack was doing in the department is being carried out in the same spirit in which he was doing it because his conception about what should be done about the problem, and it was also mine, was that we must not mollycoddle the Indians. The thing to do, in his view, was to try to find work for these people and encourage them to stand on their
4026	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration own feet, look after themselves, and become self-respecting and independent members of society. It seemed to me that Mr. Jack enjoyed the most extraordinary success in interesting employers and other people in this activity and all hon. gentlemen know how much all these activities depend upon the devotion and initiative of those who have direct charge of them.
I do hope this work is provided for adequately as I hope all the activities of the department are provided for adequately. It is because these two aspects of Indian affairs, education and economic development, seem to me to be the road to the future that I make no apology for having made special reference to them. That is in no sense meant to disparage the other very necessary activities of the department.
I am sure the hon. lady has been criticized, as I was criticized, for the unfortunate aspect of the department; that is, the necessity and obligation we as a people are under to see that the welfare of the Indians is looked after even though-
