I had just a thought or two to express before concluding and I am grateful for the indulgence of the committee for permitting me to underline the following points. I believe we must not forget the Indians are not to blame for the state in which too many of them still find themselves and that we have an inescapable obligation to see that the Indians who are not able to look after themselves are looked after in an adequate fashion. But we must also always keep before us the real objective to put them in a position where they feel they can compete with others on an equal basis. There is no doubt whatever that Indians have just as much intelligence on the average as the rest of us but what they do lack in so many cases is that feeling of confidence that comes from a certain measure of independence and above everything else this is what we must seek to give them.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit a comment


before someone else speaks. If he would permit a comment I would say that I have noted a vast difference in the ex-minister since his association with Mel Jack began.

Mr. Chairman, of all the
numerous departments of our government the one over which the hon. lady presides with such grace and distinction is to my mind one of the most important. I wish to congratulate the charming minister for the diligence and prompt attention she gives to inquiries with respect to matters under her jurisdiction which even I as a new member have been able to observe in the short few months I have had the privilege of sitting in this chamber. I have had occasion to contact the minister on several occasions, mostly by mail, and I have always received courteous and immediate attention. I have no doubt that all hon. members of this committee in their experience with it have gained the impression that this is an efficient, well-run department.
The Gordon report on Canada's economic prospects-and by the way, it is not a secret document-states that a substantial flow of immigrants is needed during the next seven or eight years to compensate for the relative scarcity of native-born entrants into the labour force. It also makes reference to the Department of Labour's estimates that in the absence of immigration in the nine years between 1946 and 1955 the labour force would have declined with a resultant retarding of our economic development.
I realize that there are arguments against immigration. One is that immigrants take jobs from the native-born and the other is that they work for less pay. I disagree with both of these opinions. Immigration creates new consumer markets and in some cases it has brought considerable capital investment and has been responsible for the establishment of new industry. And, as pointed out by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, it has been responsible for bringing in people who have made a notable contribution to the development of the country.
As for wages, immigrants from the British Isles and from Europe are not unfamiliar with trade unions. As a matter of fact, those immigrants came to us because of a desire to better their standard of living, as is the desire of any Canadian, and are therefore not a deterrent to well developed trade unions. On the contrary, they are for the most part the trade union's greatest supporters.
It should not be forgotten that the whole of Canada's prosperity has been brought about by immigration. It can be said that the development of our natural resources and the prosperity of our country as a whole

are a direct result of population. Since 1939, as the Gordon report shows:
The development has been rippling across many sectors of the economy. According to a publication known as the "Population Reference Bureau" which has been doing research work on Canada, the high ratio of resources to people places Canada in the most favourable position in the world.
Canadians are wont to compare Canada with the United States, the income, the production and the number of consumers. The Gordon report states that the United States produced 16 times as much as Canada did. There is no question that the relative position of the Canadian people will improve as the population grows. Canada has 4.3 persons per square mile in comparison with 58 per square mile in the United States; therefore, no one can say that we are overcrowded.
It is rather significant that during most of those years immigration has been averaging 120,000 a year. Now, immigration is practically at a standstill. It seems to me we should be looking forward and beyond the present setback in unemployment, which appears to be a deterrent to immigration.
Where are the plans for the development of the north? Surely this government can direct the economy to full employment and adopt a long-term policy on immigration and give immediate consideration to the lifting of the present restrictions.
Speaking of restrictions, I may say it appears to me that a more generous attitude toward immigrants from Asiatic countries should be considered, especially where there is a distinct hardship imposed on Canadian citizens of Chinese and Japanese origin, when individuals are seeking admission of certain categories of relatives which section 20(d) of the act seems to exclude, such as an older brother, a nephew, a married daughter and her family, an adopted son, a widowed sister, and so on.
My experience with people of Asiatic origin has been most happy. In Fort William we have several hundred people of Japanese and Chinese extraction, and they are the most industrious and law-abiding citizens that we have. If we broaden the ethnic origins by immigration from any and all countries it will not harm us. On the contrary, it will be beneficial. Canada's transition to a multiracial society can make only for new strength and stability. But what is even more important than the conditions of entry to Canada is the way we treat immigrants once they are admitted for permanent residence in our country. We want to make sure that all Canadians, whatever their origin, have complete equality in letter and in spirit in this nation of Canada.
Since the end of world war II more than 1J million immigrants have arrived in
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Canada. They have settled in all parts of the country, in large cities, in small towns, and in rural areas. Once they have arrived in Canada their new homeland their great and overwhelming ambition is to become Canadian citizens. The story of how these new Canadians are finally and formally inducted into the fabric of Canadian citizenship and into the responsibilities which Canadian citizenship entails is not one to which we can point with pride.
I have before me a copy of a survey of some naturalization court ceremonies held in some communities throughout the country. They more or less follow a pattern. Usually they are held in a courthouse in an uninspiring setting, with a judge saying a few words of caution, followed by a short address by some elected or appointed official, maybe the mayor or a member of parliament, or the president of the chamber of commerce. Were it not for the interest shown by members of the Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire, who are usually represented and who do try to emphasize the patriotic motive of the event by handing out a booklet on Canada, there is little to indicate the tremendous importance of the ceremony, not only to the recipient but to every Canadian.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is a lady of perception and well-versed in the activities of that wonderful organization, the I.O.D.E., which I have already mentioned. I express the hope that the government will consider the establishment of a uniform program, with suitable publicity provided for. The book which I hold in my hand, issued by the Canadian citizenship council, contains several good suggestions and from it I wish to read one or two paragraphs which indicate the study and care which went into the preparation of this book:
Could we have a ceremony ritual incorporated in the citizenship act? This could leave room for local variations, but the main items would be part of the act, simply establishing that the granting of certificates shall be by award in public, each recipient shall be accompanied by his sponsors, and the presiding judge shall follow the procedure laid down in schedule X. Representatives of local, civic and provincial authorities and organizations interested in citizenship shall be invited to attend and, where convenient, be given part in the ceremony. All of this should be set out in the act in legal phraseology.
I express the hope that the hon. lady will give serious consideration to a new approach to the reception of new Canadian citizens and a long range plan of immigration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I well realize, Mr. Chairman, that possibly the patience of the committee is getting rather limited at this point. However, I should like to take a few minutes to bring
4028	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to the attention of the minister a very important matter. I am rising on a matter of extreme urgency and I should like to appeal to the minister for immediate attention to this problem if at all possible.
It concerns the adequacy of fresh drinking water for the Indian people who live on the Eskasoni reservation in my constituency. Since 1956, two years ago, the chief of the Eskasoni band, Mr. Wilfred Prosper, has been seeking improved water facilities for his people. To illustrate this point may I read from a letter dated October 30, 1957, signed by Chief Prosper and bringing the matter to my attention. At that time he said:
Many of our people are drinking water from our brooks and marshes and many of our children have in the past been adversely affected.
May I add here that I have personally seen these people dipping water out of roadside drains. That, you will agree, is a very startling statement. Equally startling is his next statement:
Since our agent has been unsuccessful we are asking you to intercede for us as correction has been promised over a year ago.
For more than a year these Indian people have been forced to endanger their health and perhaps their lives by having to resort to drainage water after their drilled wells ceased to yield a sufficient supply or became grossly contaminated. Fortunately new sources of water have been found for them but at a considerable distance from their homes.
I brought this matter to the attention of the former minister and it is my information that the regional superintendent of Indian agencies for the maritimes conducted a full investigation. In his recommendation he stated that the only logical course of action now open to the department is to instal a proper pressure system in preference to a system of drilled wells which, in the past, has proven to be unsatisfactory.
I am cognizant of the fact that installation of such a system is not without engineering problems. I appeal to the present minister, knowing her interest in the welfare of the Indian people, to take this case under immediate advisement. The cost of extending pipe line facilities to the reservation may, I fully understand, constitute a rather expensive proposition, but I have no hesitation in recommending it to the minister's attention for two very important reasons. First, we should always be mindful of our obligations to care for our Indian people in all parts of Canada. Second, the cost of pipe lines would be an extremely modest investment if used as a means of warding off a horrible


epidemic brought about by further governmental neglect of this problem which, may I say, has been inherited by the present administration.

Mr. Chairman, I have a considerable number of questions I want to ask the minister later regarding the public archives and the national gallery but I should like to make a few remarks now and ask some questions on the citizenship and immigration part of the minister's responsibilities.
I asked a question some time ago on the order paper about the backlog of immigration applications in Italy. My question stemmed from questions asked in the house during the last session of the then minister. In essence, I interpreted what the former minister told us as meaning that one of the reasons for the backlog in Italy, which he said could not be relieved by establishing additional offices, was that there was a lack of co-operation on the part of the Italian authorities. That seemed to me to be implicit in his answer although not there in actual words.
I have spoken to a number of people of Italian background in my community and they still insist to me that one of the best things that could be done to improve Canada's immigration service in Italy would be the establishment of one or more offices in the field. I made this point the last time I had the opportunity and the minister turned it down, as I interpret it, because there was a lack of Italian co-operation. I should like to have the opinion of the present minister in this regard. I should also like to know how big the backlog is at the present time and whether it is continuing to grow.
One other factor has come to my attention affecting several Italian immigrants who have come to Canada, obtained Canadian citizenship, have then wanted to go to the United States and have sought to be placed on the quota list. Until these cases were drawn to my attention I did not know that despite the fact they are American citizens they are not treated as such by the United States government which places people on their quotas, I understand, according to national origin.
I think the hon. member made a slip of the tongue. He said "despite the fact they are American citizens". He meant Canadian citizens.

Canadian citizens. I know that the minister, because of her statements, is as anxious as I am that these people should have full Canadian rights with regard to moving to another country, but they do not have full Canadian rights. I know that the answer is, what can Canada do about it, but I wonder whether representations have been

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
made and discussions held with the United States authorities on this point and what reply they have made.
Another matter in connection with immigration that interests me has to do with whether there has been any recent improvement in the handling of people in Poland who desire to come to Canada. From the difficulties that people in this country have who are anxious to bring out relatives from Poland, it is obvious that while the Polish government is co-operating it is not doing so as fully as it might. It is also obvious that there is quite a load on the Canadian officers in Warsaw in this regard. I should like to have a statement on what the situation is at the present time in terms of difficulty and whether there has been any recent improvement.
On the topic of our Indians I was interested that the former minister under the Liberal regime should have mentioned the Pickle Crow experience. I am not surprised. I was interested to note that is one place where good work has been done because my first full time job was in the Pickle Crow area working underground. I remember that the biggest shock I ever had as a Canadian occurred at the Central Patricia mine when I walked over from the bunkhouse to the cookhouse for my first dinner. I may say that the meals were very good and there was a whole line of garbage cans outside with a considerable amount of waste. At each garbage can there were three or four Indian children and women fishing around in them. I will always remember that at the first garbage can there was a quite attractive Indian girl of about 16. A couple of cantaloup rinds and some blueberries were floating on top of the garbage and this young girl was fishing them out as if they were prizes.
It is a shock that has never left me and I have been very curious and pleased to discover just in the last six or seven months the attempts that have been made in that area to get work for some of the Indians. I know from some of the inquiries that have come in from the mine property that it is almost a mine philanthropy in a sense in that some of the miners and some of the management officers are trying to look after the aged Indians, trying to find out such things as their date of birth, and this is an especially good example.
One of the difficulties in connection with Indians doing any permanent work in the pulp and paper operations in my area is that there has been a switch in the pulp and paper operations to the use of the chain saw. The difficulty is that the chain saws are quite expensive and the Indians do not seem
to have the aptitude towards taking care of those chain saws and the general equipment that other people have. While they are good workers while they are working and can quite often turn out a pretty high cordage, it seems very difficult to give them an incentive to work steadily. The tendency is that after they cut 15 cords or 20 cords they come in and get paid for it and then they lounge around, taking it easy. It is very hard to get them to integrate into the bunkhouse set up or the dormitory set up that one has in pulp and paper operations.
In the area from Sioux Lookout east along the north line of the C.N.R. and down towards the lakehead where a great deal of pulpwood is cut, I think much more use could be made of Indians. I think it is a challenge to the Indian affairs branch to try to get them working for more companies and with greater co-operation. I think in a sense it will be a philanthropy for some time on the part of these companies doing this; it may be some time before they begin to get a real return from the Indians. I know I talked to one woods manager who told me that the only place they had really been able to get a full return from the Indians happened to be in connection with where they were cutting up some burned pulp wood stands right handy to an Indian reservation. Because there was a little bit of stability in the Indian community they turned out very good work. From my knowledge of the Indian agents in the particular region from which I come, I do not feel that they in themselves have the scope or the imagination to carry out this sort of work. In other words, I am suggesting an expansion of a kind of work that I do not believe the department has tackled up till now in any consistent way.
One of the other comments I wanted to make I received from two chiefs in that particular area. I am not going to name them or the band because they were quite specific about that; but they both feel that the Indian agents have their interest at heart, that they are in many ways kind and considerate men but that they definitely take the attitude "We know best". In the case of one chief and his band in particular, this is a fairly consistent aggravation. The minister may know from her dealings now with the Indians how hard it is to get them to give you concrete proposals that you can present to remedy things. I suppose it is just something that has to move along and grow and develop. The only suggestion I can make in this regard is that she try as best she can to get her Indian agents to subdue that attitude "We know what is best for you" and to see if they can move further along
4030	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the line of encouraging the Indians to take more responsibility for their own affairs.
I do not know whether or not the minister has read the book by a young lad who came out from England and worked as an agent at the Gull Bay Indian reserve. It is a sort of a lark. I think it is very pleasing to read. I think he stretched a long bow in certain places; but contained within the book, I think, is a fairly good indication of the Indian character, at least as it is manifested in northwestern Ontario.
I should like to see some of the best minds in the country, especially in the sociological sense, turned loose on that particular problem to see what we can do. I will not say to alter the Indian character but to get into the Indian life some of the incentives that the rest of the Canadian community accepts and at present the Indian does not. That is about all of the questions and remarks I have for now until we come to the archives.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on citizenship and immigration estimates. The city of Kitchener which is in my riding of Waterloo North is probably the greatest cosmopolitan centre of its size in Canada. Kitchener has over 500 Jewish people, 500 Polish people, 4,000 Germans and many others from foreign countries. My correspondence, as you can well understand, is made up of about 40 per cent of citizenship and immigration problems. I should like to take this opportunity of extending my sincere thanks to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for the wonderful co-operation I have received from her during this session and from those in her department. Through her efforts many families have been brought together after many years of separation. These people are becoming fine citizens of this great Canada of ours. On their behalf I again say to the minister: Thanks a million for your co-operation and that of your department.

My remarks at this time, Mr. Chairman, at this time will be rather brief. However, I should just like to say a few words on behalf of the hundreds of people who are spread throughout Europe, families that were broken up during the war and for different reasons wives and children have been unable to get to this country to join their husbands. I know that most of those people are behind the iron curtain. On their behalf I should like to make a strong appeal to the minister and use every influence she has with the Russian embassy in trying to see if we cannot get some of these people out here and get those families united again.
Like my friend the hon. member for Waterloo North, in my county, which is a


good place to live, we have a great many people who come in and a great many people who would like to come in. In my dealings with the immigration department I find that we run across a great many problems which you might say were borderline problems. You might say that I was a bit of a border problem myself when I came into this country and I realize what it is all about. I recall that when I came to this country two things were necessary. You had to be vaccinated. You had to have $15. I was vaccinated, all right, but I did not have the $15. However, my brother was with us. He went into the immigration shed first, showed his vaccination, showed his $15 and came around and pushed it through the slats to me. I then went in and we both entered for the same price. I hope the minister will not look back too much at my record or she might want to deport me.
There is another matter that I should like to raise at this time. It has to do with British subjects from Hong Kong. A number of them are trying all the time to get into this country. I think we are just a little bit hard in that respect. For one thing, they must be less than 21 years of age. I think the age limit could be raised somewhat, which would certainly help in many cases. It is rather unfortunate that a British subject should find it so hard to get into Canada when he can get into other parts of the British commonwealth quite easily.
There is another matter which I would like to bring forward and that is in connection with those immigrants who have come to Canada who are elderly people. A great many of them try from time to time to get their citizenship papers but they find that they are unable to do so because they have not been able to learn to speak the English language. I think when we are dealing with people who are getting up in years, say 60 or 70 years of age, they should have the privilege of becoming Canadian citizens before they pass on. In special cases I think the fact that they do not speak English should be overlooked.
I have not prepared a speech because I did not expect to speak at this time but I would like the minister to look into the situation with respect to families behind the iron curtain. I have in mind particularly the Chinese people who wish to bring their children and in some cases their wives or other relatives to join them in Canada but find that there is a great problem in getting them out here. I also wish to mention the problem of those people who have come to Canada from Hong Kong and I would ask that consideration be given to this whole

problem of making it easier for Asiatic people to come to Canada. I do not mean we should open the door and let them all come in but I do feel that in special cases where there is a real reason for relaxing the regulations we should not stick to technicalities.

Before proceeding, Mr. Chairman, I would like to make one or two remarks in reference to comments made in this debate. First, on the question raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate with respect to the remarks of a judge at a citizenship proceeding, I am sure we all regretted that these remarks should have been made. Whether they were actually made in the form in which they appeared in the press is, of course, open to question.
I had the same idea and that is why I did not mention the name of the judge.

I am sure there is no hon. member of this house who has not had some of his remarks misinterpreted or the wrong impression taken from them but, be that as it may, I think we might well be guided in our thinking by the words of a famous English poet who probably was not thinking of immigration when he penned those memorable lines "that man's the true cosmopolite who loves his native country best."
The hon. member for Fort William said, among other things, that there should be equality for all Canadians, and I might say that that is the motive behind the presentation of the amendment to the Citizenship Act, which I think we will be considering in this house next week.
With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Lincoln in regard to applicants for citizenship who are unable to convince the court of their knowledge of the English language, may I say that this is a matter within the discretion of the court. A judge may, if he thinks it proper, give citizenship status to these people after they have a residence of 20 years, even though they do not have what he considers to be adequate knowledge of one of the two languages of Canada.
I might suggest that that information be passed along to a great many judges who do not seem to be aware of that practice.

I would like to make one
observation and ask one or two questions of the minister. The hon. lady quoted the hon.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville. I am sure she did not intentionally misinterpret the hon. gentleman, but since she quoted his remarks I have looked at his speech and it seems to me quite clear that what he was advocating was a compulsory citizenship certificate for everyone. While I am not endorsing the hon. gentleman's remarks, I do think they make the observations of the minister beside the point.

May I just say in that
regard that the hon. member is quite right. I did misconstrue the remarks of the hon. gentleman but my offer still holds.
Oh yes, I am sure that if the hon. lady would like a little advertising for these cards-
I have one myself.

I have one of my own,
signed by myself, and I have often wondered whether it might not confuse the people at the border if I ever used it, but there are very few of us who can have that distinction-the hon. lady, Mr. Harris and myself.
The first question I wanted to ask was whether the hon. lady could say whether there are any communities in Canada other than Toronto and Montreal-that is to say large urban areas-where it would appear to be advisable to establish federal courts. I know there are outlying places where federal courts are established but I am wondering if, for instance, in Vancouver, Hamilton, Winnipeg and Edmonton-which I suppose would be the most congested places, and there may be others-the ordinary courts are adequately coping with the load of citizenship applications.
The other question I wish to ask was whether the hon. lady would indicate, because I think this would be of interest to the country, the revenue of the citizenship registration branch? In reply to the first question of the hon. member, I am personally of the opinion that this is a matter which needs great consideration.

That is to say the urban
centres?

Yes, and I have already embarked upon a study of the problem. I hope to come up with some sort of reasonable solution during my tenure of office.
With regard to the revenue of the branch, in 1956-57 it was $419,085 and in 1957-58

Just one question on this matter; I think this is the vote which includes language classes, although I am speaking from memory.
Yes.

I wonder if the hon. lady can say whether there has been any further development. There are some parts of Canada from which we have perhaps not received as much co-operation in this regard as we would have wished, and I wonder if perhaps the hon. lady had attempted to exercise her wiles on her friends in the province of Quebec, for example, to see if perhaps a little more co-operation could be obtained from the Quebec government?

Mr. Chairman, I do not normally go about my work in that fashion. I find that the latest estimate of yearly enrolment in language classes is close to 50,000 students, and the federal share of conducting those classes last year increased by 15 per cent to some $240,000. The branch has been promoting, more particularly, the establishment of new types of classes for housewives, night shift workers and immigrants awaiting job placement. The branch has also begun, with the co-operation of the various departments of education, a series of regional training seminaries for teachers in order to improve the effectiveness of instruction methods.

There was one other question. I believe one of the last actions of which I have much recollection was to authorize a research project in which the University of Toronto was interested, and I wonder if the hon. lady has any information about that.
We do not have that report just yet. When we do receive it I will be glad to let the hon. gentleman know.
Could the minister answer the question about the Canadian writers' foundation and the reason for ending the grant?

Immigration branch-
62. Administration of the Immigration Act, $1,235,232.
On item 62, if the hon. lady would like to have my questions before she answers the other ones-
Very well.

I asked a question on the order paper and the hon. lady answered it the other day. It was about Chinese immigration, whether there have been any changes in the procedure. The hon. lady said there had not been any changes since the present administration came into office. I understand that the hon. lady recently received a memorandum from the Chinese benevolent association making certain representations to the department and I wondered whether consideration of that had been completed, and if any changes were in contemplation in consequence.
I wondered also whether, now that the British West Indies Federation has been established, any steps had been taken toward reaching some kind of agreement with that federation similar to the agreements we have with India, Pakistan and Ceylon. I do not know, of course, whether it is the intention to proceed in that way. I know it had been my intention, which I discussed with my colleagues when I was in office, to take up this matter as soon as the federation was established if I was in a position to do so. I do think it would be a very good thing to do because there is a real problem here, a problem which in my opinion is not easy of solution.
Like the hon. member for Port Arthur, I am very much interested in what it is possible now to do in Poland. I do know that in the last few months I was minister because of certain things that had happened it was becoming a good deal easier for people with relatives here in Canada to get out of Poland and we were doing our utmost in the department to facilitate their entry to Canada in cases where they came within the category of relatives admitted from other European countries.
I am sure the hon. lady would not expect me to let this opportunity pass without asking her to bring me up to date on the interesting history of Mr. George Christian Hanna, the gentleman who was of great interest to the hon. lady's party and party organization, in one part of the country at least, not so very long ago.
I should also like to know in more general terms whether any change whatsoever has been made in deportation procedures since the present administration took office on June 21, and if any change has been made in the procedures for appeals in cases of deportation.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
These are some questions that occur to me, though it is possible that the hon. lady will raise more by her answers.

I have a few comments I wanted to make on immigration, but 1 think that most of these will be covered by questions. However, there is one question which has been raised by the hon. member on which I did want to make a statement. I am sure he will find that interesting, also.
I might say with regard to all these problems-Chinese immigration, people from behind the iron curtain, those who have left iron curtain countries and are in other countries but not in Canada, and the situation in Italy-we have been grappling with all these problems. We have been handicapped, of course, by the fact that the house has been sitting during the whole time that this minister has been in charge of the administration. We have discussed some of these problems, and we have come to some sort of agreement among ourselves, but we have not yet been able to put them into effect or to present them for the consideration of the government as a whole. However, on this one problem of non-immigrants in Canada we have come to a decision, and on that matter I should like to say a few words.
An increased number of non-immigrants have, after entry, applied for permanent residence in Canada. Many of them have obtained employment. A good number are from countries where, if they had applied in that country for an immigrant visa, this would have been refused.
In order to dispose of the applications now on hand, which number over 700, it has been decided to review each case. If the case appears to have merit and if the applicant can readily be absorbed into our economy, consideration will be given to recommending to the governor in council that the non-immigrant be exempted from the operation of the immigration regulations relating to admissibility for permanent residence.
Non-immigrants now in Canada who wish to remain permanently and have not yet applied will have until March 1, 1959, to submit their applications. Those who submit their applications before that date will be dealt with exactly the same as those who, as of today, have applied for permanent residence. This procedure however will not apply to persons who are now under order of deportation and whose cases have been reviewed on appeal and the appeal dismissed.
The non-immigrants who will enter Canada after today or who are now in Canada and
will apply after the first of March, 1959, will be dealt with according to the Immigration Act and regulations.
It is expected this action will permit the admission of the major portion of those applying and will eliminate misunderstandings which have created difficulties in the past. This new procedure respecting non-immigrants is a very important result of the extensive review of immigration policy and procedures begun by the government shortly after June 21, 1957, and will be a major step in the government's promise to strengthen, stabilize, and put more human understanding into this country's immigration program.
As I said before, this is a matter which has been under consideration for some time, and I am sure the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate will view it sympathetically because he knows from experience the tremendous number of problems that arise in immigration. We have still a great deal to do, but I hope we will get most of these problems solved.
I feel I must say a word or two about some statements which have been made, and while I have agreed up to now with most of the things which have been said by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I think I must remind him, as the acting minister reminded him last year, that the slowdown in immigration was instituted by the hon. gentleman himself when he was minister of citizenship and immigration.
I might mention that the hon. lady has slowed down the passage of her estimates by making that observation.
I do not intend this to be controversial, but the actual cut-off date was April 12, 1957.
Would the hon. lady like me to clear that up right now?
Go ahead.

There has been some considerable misunderstanding of this matter. I cleared it up on the day we took interim supply last October, and I cleared it up again in January, but it seems to be necessary to repeat these things a good number of times before they are understood. On April 12, 1957 I gave a direction to the department that no visas were to be issued that would be valid after July 31. As some hon. members will recall I expected to be somewhat preoccupied elsewhere than in the department between April 12 and June 10 and in fact I was. At that time I said the whole question would be reviewed after June 10. Although I was minister for 12 days after June 10 I felt this was a proper matter for review by my successor; but there was
4034	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration nothing which restricted immigration up to the time the former administration went out of office.
It was apparent by April 12 that there was going to be an unprecedently large immigration in the year 1957 and, as I said earlier, it turned out to be the biggest year since 1913. I believe I was properly apprehensive that we might find in the autumn more people than could obtain work. I thought it was wise at that time to indicate that visas should not be granted for travel to Canada after July 31 but that, of course, would have been subject to review in the light of conditions that existed in the latter part of June. As I say, circumstances developed which made it seem to me improper for me to review that matter.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman has been misunderstood there has been no more misunderstanding of his action than his interpretation of the actions of former governments in the thirties. On this point the hon. member for Fort William described immigration as being practically at a standstill. I believe those were his words. I should like to say this is a misconception of the actual conditions. Up until June 30 of this year there were 67,744 immigrants received into Canada. I would scarcely call that a standstill.
Would the hon. lady give the corresponding figure for 1957?

Surely, Mr. Chairman. The year 1957 was exceptional. There were 282,164 immigrants admitted during the entire year, 182,000 of them during the first six months. But going back to 1956 only 69,900 were admitted in the first six months, only about 2,000 more than were admitted in the first six months of this year. Approximately 58,000 entered in the first six months of 1955, nearly 10,000 less than were admitted during the first half of the current year.
Mr. Chairman, doubtless the hon. lady will recall that that was the year she and her colleague on this side of the house were putting on a big campaign about unemployment.

That was not the reason, Mr. Chairman. In fact, it does not make much difference what the reason is and if the hon. gentleman wishes to cite reasons for these developments we could go back a long way but I have one eye on the clock and would like to get these estimates through if possible. We admitted to Canada approximately 10,000 more immigrants in the first six months of 1958 than were admitted during the first six months of 1955.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to know if these applications were approved this year?
These immigrants actually entered this year.
Actual entries, not applications?
They actually landed in Canada in the first six months of this year.
My question is were these applications approved this year?
Well, some of them, I presume, would have been approved last year and it takes a while for them to be processed and for the immigrants to journey to Canada.
Yes, that is the point. How many months will it take for applications to be processed and approved?

It depends on where
they come from. For instance, in the case of Italy it takes some time and we have a backlog from Italy of nearly 60,000.
That is precisely the point I was making, Mr. Chairman. Applications are not being approved at the present time. Many who entered this year would have had their applications approved last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?
No, Mr. Chairman. I asked the hon. lady a considerable number of questions and I expect answers to them.
I was under the impression that I had answered all the questions on immigration problems although I grant you I grouped several together.
No, Mr. Chairman. For example, the hon. lady did not give me the latest chapter in the history of Mr. Hanna.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, and I apologize for that oversight. I had that notation on a separate piece of paper, Mr. Hanna, as hon. gentlemen know, was tried for an offence and as is the case with all persons tried in Canada he had the right of appeal. We extended his stay, I believe until August 15. Finally, in the last few days before he would have been due to depart, he entered an appeal. I understand he had some difficulty trying to secure legal support for his appeal and having failed to do so he filed the appeal himself. It is my understanding that the matter comes up for review in September and of course until that time it is before the courts.

I am going to ask the hon. lady if she will appeal to her colleague and supporter in the house, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who was so very anxious to give Mr. Hanna legal help at a time when he was seeking illegal entry to Canada, and suggest that it is certainly a moral obligation upon that hon. member to offer his services as a lawyer to Mr. Hanna in this appeal. I also asked the hon. lady about deportation procedures generally and if there had been any change since last year.
No, Mr. Chairman, not since last year. It is one of many problems with which we are grappling at the present time.

I should now like to make a comment or two about the announcement made by the hon. lady. What her announcement amounted to when stripped of all its verbiage is that instead of considering each application individually as has been the case in the past she is attempting to establish a cut-off date so as to consider all these cases at once and then apply all the full rigours of the law after March 1. Having dealt with those cases as they arose over a period of some three years, I can understand why any minister would seek to formalize the procedure and reduce the amount of agony connected with it, but I would not like the hon. lady to get away with the impression that this represents any liberalization of the policy of the department because it is in fact the precise reverse. I do not think she will be successful in maintaining her cut-off date but, of course, I do not blame her for trying. We all have to try these things and learn from experience.
There is one other question I should like to ask the hon. lady that occurred to me as she was talking and it is this. Is she satisfied with the efficiency of the immigration branch and of the employees in the branch, speaking generally? I ask that question because when the hon. lady was on this side of the house-I do not know that she did herself but a considerable number of her colleagues on this side of the house and a considerable number of their supporters outside the house-spent a great deal of their time talking about the heartless bureaucracy and the soulless officials in the immigration branch. I always thought this was the most unfair and unwarranted kind of criticism. I never minded the criticism of the heartlessness of the minister because I could reply to that, but I thought the attack on the immigration branch as being composed of a particularly soulless lot of bureaucrats was most unfair because I do not know any more devoted group of public servants anywhere
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration in the public service of Canada than those who work in the immigration branch. I wish to pay them this tribute as their former minister. I wondered if on closer acquaintance with the department the minister did not find that in this respect at least I was right?
Mr. Chairman, I never said a word of that kind on this subject in this house. I think the hon. member's remarks are out of place but in any event he answered himself.
Mr. Chairman, I am not interested in answering myself. I would like the hon. lady's answer.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to turn the discussion of these estimates into a court of inquiry into the activities of the employees of the immigration branch.

Mr. Chairman, on a point
of order-
Sit down.

I think the hon. lady must be forgetting where she is. We are the elected representatives of the people. The hon. lady is one of Her Majesty's advisors charged with carrying out the functions of a particular department of the federal government. She is here craving supply to carry on her department. It is the duty especially of those elected to oppose the government to carry on an inquisition into the efficiency of every department. That is what we are elected for and what we intend to do.
This is an example of arrogance which I had not expected from the hon. lady; this is a display such as we never had from the gentleman who used to sit in the seat in which she is sitting at this very moment. In all my experience in this house I can never remember that gentleman saying that other members of the house were not entitled to ask questions about the administration of his department. It is true that he occasionally became a little impatient with the constant repetition of questions but he never suggested that the opposition did not have the right to ask him questions. I can assure you, sir, that just so long as there are members to interrupt me, and spell me off and just so long as I have questions to ask about the immigration branch-and I do not care whether they are called an inquisition or anything else-I will go on carrying out the duty for which I was elected and ask those questions. I repeat my question. I ask the honourable lady whether she is satisfied with the efficiency of the employees of the immigration branch, and I feel I am entitled to an answer.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

Mr. Chairman, I submit to hon. members that that is not a fair question. I have answered all the hon. member's questions to the best of my ability, but when he groups a large number of people, 2,000 people, and asks me whether I am completely satisfied with each and every one of them, it is a question which I could not possibly answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Idiotic.

I can assure the hon. member that if I find there are people in my department who are inefficient I will take appropriate action. The fact that they are there means one of two things, either that I am satisfied with their activities or that I have not heard about them yet.

I must say that the hon. lady has given a very clever and very effective reply and I give her full marks. But still she would not expect me to let her put words in my mouth. I did not ask her whether she was completely satisfied with every employee. I will phrase my question in the way I meant it to be understood. Perhaps I was a little sloppy in phrasing it. But I ask her, is she satisfied after-the months go on; is it three months, the hon. lady would know how long she has been the minister-three months and more with the efficiency of the immigration branch?

Mr. Chairman, it is very hard to answer that question without going into the whole field of immigration policy. Let me say I am not satisfied with the policy generally. If I were, I would not have been taking part in the various discussions and investigations on which I reported a few minutes ago. There are a great many things that still need to be done. In so far as the efficiency of the civil service is concerned, I think by and large most of our civil servants are extremely efficient individuals.
That is the answer I expected.

I would like to ask the minister to answer the questions I put in connection with one immigration office in Italy and also with regard to the attitude towards naturalized Canadians, also the situation in Poland and in Finland.

I thought I had answered the questions with regard to Poland. They are all a part of the over-all immigration policy which we are considering very carefully. The manner of the entry of naturalized Canadians into the United States is not properly a problem of this department. If

the question were put to any department of government it should be put to external affairs.
With regard to the question on Italy, last year in round figures we had a backlog of about 45,000. This year we have a backlog of 60,000 in the one office. One of the difficulties of opening other offices is that we fear it would just create a larger and larger backlog because of the greater facilities to receive applications. We hope that because of the considerations of policy which are under way at the present time we may find a solution to this great problem.

I hope the minister does. I think she will recognize the contribution the hon. member for Fort William made, the more people we get out from that fine country the better. Since we have the legal opportunities for them to come to this country or, at least, the openings, as a result of government policies, it is a pity that some of them cannot take advantage of it.
On the question of the United States quota system, the minister has expressed her interest in making the naturalized Canadian citizenship as good as the full Canadian, that is, the Canadian who was born here. I think that is the intent of her legislation. Well, surely, citizenship is something that you can carry abroad with you, and in that sense could this question of the United States quota not be something that she could consider? I mean, follow it up and ask external affairs to take up the matter. I was curious as to whether there had ever been any discussion with the United States on this particular point.

Mr. Chairman, it would seem to be not quite proper for us to try to dictate the immigration policy of another country but I am quite willing to explore the matter with the Department of External Affairs to see whether they can make representations in that regard. But, as the hon. member said himself, the United States policy is based on a different conception from ours, and they go on the country of origin, as the hon. member has said.

It still remains, Mr. Chairman, a fact that I would like the minister to look into it.
I would like to raise another important point, which is a matter of keen interest to me. Two Canadians are living side by side; one a native-born and the other is a naturalized Canadian. They decide to go to the United States. The minister must recognize that one is in a much better position to get in. Surely, that impinges upon the worth of our citizenship.

The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate asked the minister some questions with regard to the brief submitted by the Chinese benevolent association, dated July 25, 1958. I just want to speak for a few minutes. I am not in any hurry. This is a brief of some 13 pages, which is very well prepared by the persons in this excellent benevolent association. I have very carefully read it and I do not intend to read it completely this afternoon, but I do urge the minister to give very serious consideration to their representations for some extension of the regulations wtih respect to the admission of relatives. I have one other matter, and I mention it purely because of the fact that when the minister was in opposition several of her colleagues supported briefs similar to this when they were brought to the attention of the government of the day. I wish to say that in my experience I find that these Chinese people are very popular with the population in general. There were early settlers in our district and had a lot to do with early gold mining; they were cooks in labour camps; they were in steam-boating, laundries, vegetable gardening and things of that sort. I do not know of any group that is more popular as a long-time residence group than the older Chinese in my constituency. I do hope the minister will give very serious consideration to their representations. I say that because the present Minister without Portfolio was one of the ministers who spoke very favourably of their representations and the present Minister of National Defence also supported their representations. The present Minister of Justice was very sympathetic towards the views of these people.
But I do want to bring to the minister's attention one thing that struck me. I think they have to go at the present time to some territory under the control of the nationalist Chinese government and they are not accepted in Hong Kong. I cannot find the reference just now but they made some representations with respect to the place of application. Then they mention that the number of officers in Hong Kong is too small to deal with the applications and that prospective immigrants have had to wait from 5 months to more than a year before being examined. The brief goes on to propose that the number of immigration officials be substantially increased. Would the minister inform the house if the government is giving serious consideration to the representations of the Chinese benevolent association and if she has any opinion with respect to the shortage of officers in her department's office in Hong Kong?

Mr. Chairman, when I answered a few minutes ago with regard to the general problems of immigration I meant it to be understood that this was one of the very trying problems we are trying to solve. We have had representations not only from the Chinese benevolent association but also from other groups of Chinese and Japanese. The department is very carefully considering all of the representations that have been made and, as I said, it is one of the problems we are trying to solve at the present time.

I want to bring to the minister's attention a letter written to me which I think suggests somewhat of a compromise with regard to the more or less emphatic views expressed by the former minister of citizenship and immigration with respect to Canadian born immigrants and latecomers. I think there is an idea in this letter in view of the fact that there are numbers of these children who should be cared for. The letter was written to me by Mr. Charles H. Bebbington, a very well known person in Kootenay West. In it he says:
Having been in the position to observe Canadian immigration policies over a period of 60 years I would like to submit the following impressions and suggestions.
In the early days we were chiefly concerned with getting immigrants who could do heavy physical work such as building our railroads, clearing our forests, etc. Now, owing to the great advances in mechanical production methods, this class of immigrant is not so necessary. But Canada still has plenty of room for good immigrants and I think that a method that has not been tried would avoid some of the errors of past systems.
Why could we not select orphan children from European countries, build boarding schools in which to keep and educate them and bring them up to a natural Canadian citizenship? When old enough to start work they would be able to give Canada 40 to 50 years, their best years, before becoming a charge on the country because of old age. Unlike the adult immigrant they would not have to change from their native methods of work or living conditions and the language barrier would be eliminated through their childhood environment.
Canada can afford to take time to do this now as we are not desperately in need of adult immigrants. In fact it has been suggested in many quarters that the brakes be put on mainly because of the adverse effect on our labour market. By the scheme I am suggesting we would still be getting immigrants who would in due course fit perfectly into our social set-up and would automatically assume all the rights and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
This would appear to be a better way to help unfortunate children of the world than by sending money out of Canada to help them. We are proud of Canadian-made goods; these children would be Canadian-made citizens and, if carefully selected, should give strength to the country of their adoption.
Some will say that we are having difficulty educating our own children. If more stress were to be put on training these children for work in useful trades we would have little difficulty in finding places for well trained artisans. We want young citizens for a young country.
